it requires exercising exactly the skills discussed in Section 2 of this
chapter---identifying a genuine gap, building a compelling background,
and articulating specific, achievable aims with the kinds of strong
action verbs and realistic contingency planning that distinguish mature
scientific thinking from enthusiasm alone.

\subsection{NIH Individual Fellowship
Awards}\label{nih-individual-fellowship-awards}

For graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in the biomedical
sciences, the NIH offers a family of individual fellowship mechanisms
known collectively as the F series. The F31 award, the Ruth L.
Kirschstein National Research Service Award for Individual Predoctoral
Fellows, supports doctoral candidates pursuing dissertations in
health-related research\textsuperscript{173}. There is also an F31
Diversity supplement specifically designed to enhance representation of
individuals from groups underrepresented in biomedical research,
including racial and ethnic minorities and individuals with
disabilities. The F32 award supports postdoctoral researchers, providing
a structured opportunity to develop independent research skills under
the mentorship of a sponsor during the critical transition period
between doctoral training and independent faculty positions.

Unlike the GRFP, which is evaluated primarily on the strength of the
applicant's ideas and potential, NIH fellowship applications involve a
more elaborate review process that takes into account the proposed
research project, the applicant's background and qualifications, the
mentor's qualifications and track record, the training plan, and the
environment in which the training will occur\textsuperscript{183}. This
means that the quality of the mentorship relationship---and the mentor's
willingness to invest time in co-developing the fellowship
application---matters enormously. Students planning to apply for an F31
should initiate conversations with their mentor about the application
well in advance of any deadline, ideally at least a year before the
intended submission, because developing a strong individual development
plan and a coherent research proposal requires sustained collaboration
between the trainee and their sponsor.

\subsection{NNF Graduate and Postgraduate
Fellowship}\label{nnf-graduate-and-postgraduate-fellowship}

For students whose research sits at the intersection of biology and
agricultural or food systems, the USDA-NIFA National Needs Graduate and
Postgraduate Fellowship (NNF) program represents a directly relevant and
often overlooked federal opportunity. Unlike the GRFP or NIH F-series
awards, NNF fellowships are administered through individual colleges and
universities rather than applied for directly by students---meaning that
the entry point is a conversation with your department or graduate
program about whether your institution holds an active NNF grant in your
area. Awards provide stipends and travel support for master's and
doctoral students in national-need subject areas identified by NIFA,
which have historically included genomics, bioinformatics applied to
agriculture, food safety, environmental science, and natural resources.
For students at a land-grant institution like Auburn, where the USDA
relationship is institutionally deep and research programs in
agricultural genomics and computational biology are well established, it
is worth asking whether an NNF training grant is available in your
college before looking exclusively to NIH or NSF for fellowship support.

\subsection{Professional Society Grants and Other
Opportunities}\label{professional-society-grants-and-other-opportunities}

Beyond the major federal fellowships, a rich ecosystem of professional
society grants and foundation-sponsored awards provides additional
funding opportunities for graduate students and early-career
researchers. Sigma Xi, the scientific research honor society, offers
Grants in Aid of Research (GIAR) that provide modest awards---typically
up to one thousand dollars---for travel to field sites or the purchase
of equipment necessary to complete a specific research
project\textsuperscript{173}. These awards are small enough that they
fall within reach of students early in their training, but competitive
enough that earning one represents a genuine credential. The Society for
Study of Evolution, the Genetics Society of America, the Society for
Integrative and Comparative Biology, and many other discipline-specific
societies offer analogous small grants, travel awards, and presentation
fellowships.

The Phycological Society of America, for example, offers grants in aid
of research for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers
conducting work in phycology, while the American Association of
University Women provides dissertation fellowships and international
fellowships supporting women in science at the doctoral level. National
databases maintained by organizations such as Pathways to Science and
UCLA's graduate funding portal maintain searchable listings of
opportunities for MS and PhD students across disciplines, including
travel grants, writing grants, and research awards that many students
never discover simply because they do not know to look for them. The
lesson here is that the funding landscape is both broader and more
diverse than most students realize, and even awards that seem peripheral
to your primary research area can contribute to your professional
development and your CV in meaningful ways.

Making a habit of monitoring funding opportunities throughout your
graduate training---building a personal calendar of relevant deadlines,
discussing opportunities with your mentor and with advanced graduate
students in your program, and setting aside time each semester to
evaluate which competitions are most aligned with your current stage of
training and scientific focus---is itself a form of professional
practice that will pay dividends throughout your career. The scientists
who build the most robust and sustained research programs are almost
universally those who learned early to think strategically about
funding, to write clearly and compellingly about their ideas, and to
treat the peer review process not as an adversarial obstacle but as a
community conversation about what science is most worth doing.

\section{Conclusion}\label{conclusion}

Grant funding is, at its core, a conversation between scientists about
what questions matter and who is best positioned to answer them.
Understanding the history of that conversation---from the Morrill Act's
vision of practical education for working people to Vannevar Bush's
vision of science as an endless frontier to the global network of
federal agencies, private foundations, and professional societies that
funds research today---helps you see yourself not as a supplicant asking
for money but as a participant in a long and consequential tradition of
publicly supported inquiry. The skills developed by writing grant
proposals, by serving as a reviewer, and by navigating the peer review
system are among the most durable and transferable skills in science,
and there is no better time to begin developing them than during your
training. The hidden curriculum revealed in this chapter is simply this:
the scientists who thrive are those who learn to communicate the
significance of their work not just to themselves but to the entire
community that depends on good science being done well.

\section{Practice Problem Sets}\label{practice-problem-sets-2}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Proposal Identification Exercise}: Return to
  the\textsuperscript{3} paper we have read throughout the semester and,
  using the \href{https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/simple-search/}{NSF
  Award database}, identify one of the funded grants that supported the
  work described. Examine the project abstract available through NSF.
  What elements of the proposal structure described in
  Figure~\ref{fig-grantanatomy} can you identify in the abstract alone?
  What is missing from the abstract that would be present in the full
  proposal? What other publications have been produced as a result of
  this research?
\item
  \textbf{Specific Aims Practice}: Return to your narrative submitted
  for \href{Lab02.qmd}{Lab 2}. Visit the link of action verbs and try to
  write specific aims for your hypothetical research project. Expand
  your narrative to a specific aims page, which is a 1-page mini
  proposal. Your aims page should include a brief statement of the
  central problem and gap in knowledge, two to three specific aims each
  written with a strong action verb, and a closing statement of expected
  impact. Exchange your draft with a classmate and provide written
  feedback specifically addressing whether the aims are logically
  independent, whether the action verbs are sufficiently specific, and
  whether the impact statement is convincing.
\item
  \textbf{Reviewer Perspective Exercise}: Obtain two or three funded
  grant abstracts from \href{https://report.nih.gov/}{NIH Reporter} in
  your area of interest and evaluate each one against NIH's five core
  review criteria (Significance, Investigator, Innovation, Approach,
  Environment). Write a brief mock critique for each, identifying one
  major strength and one potential weakness for each criterion. Then
  compare your critiques with a classmate: where do you agree, and where
  do you disagree? What does the disagreement tell you about the
  subjective elements of peer review?
\item
  \textbf{Study Section Role Play}: In preparation for the class mock
  study section, read the assigned proposal carefully and prepare both a
  written critique and a two-minute oral summary of the major
  score-driving issues. Your oral summary should state your preliminary
  score or rating, describe the most important strengths, identify the
  most important weaknesses, and explain how you weighted those factors
  in arriving at your assessment. After the panel discussion, reflect in
  writing on whether your rating changed, why or why not, and what
  aspect of the discussion most influenced your thinking.
\item
  \textbf{Funding Landscape Map}: Using the resources described in
  Section 11.5 plus the \href{pathwaystoscience.org}{Pathways to Science
  database}, compile a personal funding calendar listing at least five
  fellowship or grant opportunities relevant to your stage of training
  and research area. For each opportunity, record the award name,
  sponsoring organization, eligibility requirements, award amount, and
  typical deadline. Present your calendar to a small group and discuss
  which opportunity you would prioritize and why.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Reflection Questions}\label{reflection-questions-9}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Vannevar Bush argued in 1945 that government should fund the ``best
  science'' without regard for geographic distribution, while Senator
  Kilgore argued for broad-based, democratically accountable support.
  Both positions have continued to shape funding policy for more than 75
  years. Where do you see the tension between these two visions playing
  out in the current funding landscape, and which perspective do you
  find more compelling? How might your answer change depending on
  whether you are thinking as a scientist, a taxpayer, or a citizen of a
  small state?
\item
  The Morrill Act of 1862 established land-grant universities with an
  explicitly democratic mission: to open higher education to farmers and
  working people by focusing on practical agriculture, science, and
  engineering. How does this original mission connect to the research
  you are doing or hope to do? In what ways does the modern research
  university, funded partly through NIFA and Hatch Act capacity grants,
  honor or depart from the vision that Justin Morrill and Abraham
  Lincoln made law?
\item
  Section 11.3 describes the specific aims page as arguably the most
  important page in a grant proposal. Think about a piece of research
  you are currently involved in or are familiar with from the
  literature. How would you translate that work into three specific
  aims, each framed around a strong action verb? What does the exercise
  reveal about the difference between describing what scientists did and
  proposing what scientists will do?
\item
  Imagine a study section or review panel where an application opened
  with uniformly enthusiastic scores from assigned reviewers but ended
  with mediocre scores after unassigned reviewers pointed out multiple
  independent weaknesses. What would this sequence of events reveal
  about the potential gap between an author's perception of their own
  work and a panel's collective evaluation of it? How might you use this
  insight to improve your own grant proposals or scientific writing more
  broadly?
\item
  This chapter presents both the NIH and NSF review frameworks because
  scientists in biology and bioinformatics encounter both during their
  careers. After participating in the class mock panel using NSF
  criteria, reflect on the differences you notice between evaluating
  proposals through the lens of Intellectual Merit alone versus the
  five-criteria NIH framework. Which system felt more natural to you as
  a reviewer, and which would you find more useful as feedback on your
  own proposals? What does your preference reveal about your scientific
  values or communication strengths?
\end{enumerate}

\section{References}\label{references-10}

\chapter{Population Genomics}\label{population-genomics}

\section{Introduction}\label{introduction-2}

As first introduced in Chapter 8, \textbf{population genomics} typically
describes a DNA resequencing project of multiple individuals from the
same population of a species. As a field, population genomics brings
together evolutionary theory and genome‑scale data to ask how mutation,
recombination, genetic drift, migration, and natural selection shape
patterns of genetic variation across the
genome\textsuperscript{188,189}. Rather than focusing on single loci,
population genomics characterizes the ``genomic landscape'' of diversity
and differentiation, providing a richer picture of how genomes evolve in
natural populations\textsuperscript{188}. This chapter introduces the
historical roots of population genomics, the key summary statistics and
evolutionary processes that govern genomic variation, and modern
genome‑wide analysis strategies such as sliding‑window and spline‑based
approaches.

The goal is to provide a broad conceptual overview rather than a
mathematically exhaustive treatment. Readers interested in formal
derivations and deeper theory are encouraged to consult dedicated
population genetics textbooks, such as Graham Coop's \emph{Population
and Quantitative Genetics} notes, which develop the underlying models
and statistical machinery in detail\textsuperscript{189}. Here, I
emphasize intuitive explanations, connections to earlier chapters (e.g.,
sequence analysis, variant calling, and alignment), and links to labs in
which you will interpret population genomic statistics such as
nucleotide diversity \(\pi\), Tajima's D, and \(F_{ST}\).

\section{From the Modern Synthesis to Population
Genomics}\label{from-the-modern-synthesis-to-population-genomics}

\subsection{Biological evolution and the forces of
change}\label{biological-evolution-and-the-forces-of-change}

Evolution is the change in allele frequency over time, typically
measured in the context of a genetic population. A population is made up
of a set of interbreeding individuals whose collective genomes
constitute its genetic composition\textsuperscript{189}. This
composition shifts because individuals are born and die, because some
individuals migrate in or out, and because individuals vary in how many
offspring they leave. Every new individual born into the population
subtly changes things: their genome is a unique combination of their
parents' genomes, shuffled by segregation and recombination during
meiosis, and possibly altered by new mutations. These individual events
seem small, but the accumulation of changes across individuals and
generations --- compounded over tens, hundreds, and millions of
generations --- produces the remarkable diversity of life on
Earth\textsuperscript{189}.

\textbf{Population genetics} is the study of the genetic composition of
natural populations and its evolutionary causes and
consequences\textsuperscript{189}. Population genomics extends this to
genome-wide data, asking how mutation, recombination, genetic drift,
migration, and natural selection together shape patterns of variation
across entire genomes\textsuperscript{188}. To understand how these
forces interact, population geneticists develop mathematical models. As
the statistician George Box famously put it, ``All models are wrong but
some are useful'' --- and the models of population genetics, despite
their simplifying assumptions, yield surprisingly accurate predictions
about patterns of genetic diversity in nature\textsuperscript{189}.

The five major forces that shape allele frequencies
are\textsuperscript{189,190}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Mutation}: Introduces new alleles at a low rate
  (\textasciitilde{}\(10^{-8}\) per base pair per generation in humans);
  the ultimate source of all genetic variation.
\item
  \textbf{Genetic drift}: Random fluctuations in allele frequencies
  caused by the finite number of individuals that survive and reproduce
  each generation; strongest in small populations.
\item
  \textbf{Migration (gene flow)}: The movement of individuals and their
  alleles between populations; tends to homogenize allele frequencies
  across geographic space.
\item
  \textbf{Recombination}: Shuffles alleles within chromosomes during
  meiosis, breaking down associations between nearby variants.
\item
  \textbf{Natural selection}: Non-random, directional change in allele
  frequencies based on differences in survival and reproduction among
  genotypes.
\end{itemize}

Understanding population genomics means understanding how these forces
operate individually, how they interact, and how to distinguish their
signatures in genomic data.

\subsection{The modern synthesis: reconciling Mendel and
Darwin}\label{the-modern-synthesis-reconciling-mendel-and-darwin}

The conceptual foundations of population genomics lie in the early
twentieth-century \textbf{modern synthesis}, which reconciled Mendelian
genetics with Darwin's theory of natural selection\textsuperscript{189}.
Darwin's theory required heritable variation and differential
reproductive success, but he had no mechanistic theory of inheritance.
Mendel provided particulate, discrete heritable factors (what we now
call alleles), but his `factors' initially seemed incompatible with the
continuous phenotypic variation --- height, weight, skin tone ---
observed in nature. The breakthrough came from Fisher, Wright, and
Haldane, who showed mathematically that Mendelian segregation at many
loci, each with small effects, produces smooth continuous phenotypic
distributions, and that changes in allele frequencies under selection
follow well-defined rules\textsuperscript{189}.

It is worth appreciating how conceptually remarkable this is. Many of
the core models of population genetics were developed in the
1920s--1940s, before anyone knew that DNA was the molecule of
heredity\textsuperscript{189}. Yet these models have only grown in power
and relevance as molecular data became available. This is because they
are built on the logic of Mendelian transmission rules combined with
probability theory --- a foundation that holds regardless of the
physical nature of heredity.

Fisher formalized the relationship between genetic variation and
evolution in his \textbf{Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection},
which links the rate of increase in mean fitness to the amount of
additive genetic variance for fitness\textsuperscript{190}. This
synthesis laid the groundwork for connecting patterns of genetic
variation in populations to the action of selection, drift, mutation,
and migration. Building on these ideas came the modern evolutionary
synthesis more broadly, integrating insights from paleontology,
systematics, and ecology into a unified picture of how both short-term
evolutionary change and the long-term diversification of life can be
explained by the gradual accumulation of genetic changes within and
among populations\textsuperscript{189}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, rightrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, toprule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Eugenics, Population Genetics, and Scientific Racism}, left=2mm, colback=white, bottomtitle=1mm, toptitle=1mm, bottomrule=.15mm, coltitle=black, titlerule=0mm, breakable, opacityback=0, arc=.35mm]

\emph{Note: The goal of this section is to situate the field of
population genetics in its historical context in a factual, objective
way, without assigning blame or asking students to endorse any
particular viewpoint.}

The history of genetics and evolutionary biology is intertwined with the
history of eugenics and scientific racism. Francis Galton coined the
term \emph{eugenics} in 1883 to describe ``human improvement'' through
controlled breeding\textsuperscript{189,191}. Eugenic thinking rested on
the idea that certain groups were genetically ``inferior'' and that
social inequalities could be justified as biological
facts\textsuperscript{191,192}. In the late nineteenth and early
twentieth centuries, eugenicists used emerging tools in statistics and
heredity to support policies restricting immigration and discouraging or
preventing reproduction by people labeled
``unfit''\textsuperscript{189,191}. In the United States, compulsory
sterilization laws disproportionately affected Black, Latino,
Indigenous, poor, and disabled individuals\textsuperscript{189,193};
coerced sterilization of Native American women continued into the
1970s\textsuperscript{194}, California prison inmates were sterilized
without lawful consent as recently as 2010\textsuperscript{195}, and a
Tennessee judge was formally reprimanded in 2017 for offering reduced
sentences in exchange for sterilization\textsuperscript{196}.

Many early geneticists engaged actively with eugenics, and major
scientific institutions have roots in the movement. The Cold Spring
Harbor Laboratory hosted a Eugenics Record Office from 1910 to
1940\textsuperscript{197}, and the journal now known as \emph{Annals of
Human Genetics} was called \emph{Annals of Eugenics} until
1954\textsuperscript{189}. R.A. Fisher devoted substantial sections of
his landmark 1930 book to eugenic arguments\textsuperscript{189,198},
and H.J. Muller framed genetic diversity in some populations as a burden
to be managed through his work on mutational load\textsuperscript{199}.
The Mendelian framework was itself selectively distorted to support
eugenic claims before geneticists pushed back on its
misuse\textsuperscript{200}.

At the same time, geneticists including Thomas Hunt Morgan and Lancelot
Hogben criticized eugenic claims, emphasizing the importance of
environment and the complexity of inheritance\textsuperscript{189}.
After World War II, explicit state-sponsored eugenics programs lost
formal legitimacy, though coercive practices persisted for decades.
Lewontin's landmark 1972 analysis showed that roughly 85\% of human
genetic variation occurs \emph{within} populations rather than between
them\textsuperscript{189,201,202}, reaffirmed many times since with
larger genomic datasets. This work helped establish that human genetic
differences, while real and scientifically interesting, do not map
neatly onto rigid racial categories or justify treating any group as
inherently superior or inferior.

Communicating this accurately remains an ongoing responsibility for
geneticists, educators, and clinicians --- including genetic counselors
--- who encounter genomic information in professional practice. Some
groups continue to selectively misuse population-genetic results, making
clear and contextualized science communication
essential\textsuperscript{189,203}. The field of genetic counseling
itself emerged, in part, as a deliberate effort to move clinical
genetics away from eugenic paternalism and toward patient-centered,
non-directive care --- a foundational value documented in the
profession's own history\textsuperscript{192,204}.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{The language of population genetics: loci, alleles, and
frequencies}\label{the-language-of-population-genetics-loci-alleles-and-frequencies}

Before going further, it helps to establish the basic vocabulary of
population genetics precisely, because these terms are used more
carefully here than in a typical introductory genetics course.

A \textbf{locus} (plural: \emph{loci}) is a specific position in the
genome\textsuperscript{189}. It could be a single nucleotide base pair
or an entire gene region. The different genetic variants that can occupy
a locus are called \textbf{alleles}. If every individual in the
population carries the same allele at a locus, that locus is
\textbf{monomorphic} --- there is no genetic variation at that position.
If two or more alleles exist in the population, the locus is
\textbf{polymorphic} (also called a \textbf{segregating
site})\textsuperscript{189}.

We call the less common allele at a polymorphic site the \textbf{minor
allele} and the more common one the \textbf{major allele}. We also
distinguish the \textbf{derived allele} (the evolutionarily newer one,
which arose by mutation) from the \textbf{ancestral allele} (the older
one, typically inferred by comparison to an outgroup
species)\textsuperscript{189}. This distinction matters when computing
the site frequency spectrum and interpreting patterns of variation.

Because we typically work with diploid organisms, every individual
carries two alleles at each autosomal locus. The \textbf{allele
frequency} is the proportion of all copies of the locus in the
population that carry a given allele. If we genotype \(N\) diploid
individuals at a biallelic locus. Based on some locus \(A\), we can
denote the number of homozygous individuals for the \(A_1\) allele as
\(N_{11}\) and the number of heterozygous individuals as \(N_{12}\),
meaning that they have both the \(A_1\) allele and the \(A_2\) allele.
The frequency of \(A_1\), is then based on the number of \(N_{11}\)
homozygotes for allele \(A_1\) and \(N_{12}\) heterozygotes, which is
calculated using the following equation:

\[
p = \frac{2N_{11} + N_{12}}{2N},
\]

and the frequency of the alternate allele \(A_2\) is simply
\(q = 1 - p\). This formula follows directly from counting allele copies
and holds regardless of Hardy--Weinberg equilibrium.

\subsection{Allozymes and the discovery of abundant molecular
variation}\label{allozymes-and-the-discovery-of-abundant-molecular-variation}

The advent of protein gel electrophoresis in the 1960s brought the first
systematic surveys of molecular genetic variation. Hubby and Lewontin,
working in \emph{Drosophila pseudoobscura}, and Harris, in humans, used
\textbf{allozyme} variation --- electrophoretically distinguishable
forms of enzymes --- to estimate heterozygosity and the proportion of
polymorphic loci without pre-selecting genes known to be
variable\textsuperscript{190}. Their surveys were a revelation: many
loci were polymorphic and individuals were heterozygous at a substantial
fraction of loci, in stark contrast to the earlier view that wild
populations were nearly monomorphic\textsuperscript{190}.

These studies introduced key summary statistics that remain central
today\textsuperscript{190}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Proportion polymorphic \(P\)}: The fraction of loci with more
  than one allele in the sample.
\item
  \textbf{Average heterozygosity \(\bar{H}\)}: The expected probability
  that a randomly chosen individual is heterozygous at a randomly chosen
  locus, averaged across loci.
\end{itemize}

A striking and puzzling pattern emerged: levels of allozyme variation
were broadly similar across species with vastly different census
population sizes\textsuperscript{190,205}. A sea squirt with billions of
individuals and a lynx with far fewer showed far less difference in
heterozygosity than their census sizes would predict. This helped
motivate the \textbf{neutral theory of molecular evolution} (Kimura,
1968), which proposes that most molecular variants are selectively
neutral or nearly neutral and that genetic drift, rather than natural
selection, governs their frequencies\textsuperscript{189,205}.

Allozymes were also instrumental in formalizing population structure.
Wright's \(F_{ST}\) quantifies genetic differentiation among
populations. Lewontin's early applications to human allozymes showed
that the vast majority (\textasciitilde85\%) of human genetic variation
occurs within populations rather than between them --- a finding with
profound implications for how we understand the relationship between
human genetic diversity and socially constructed racial
categories\textsuperscript{190}.

\subsection{From allozymes to DNA sequences and the ADH
locus}\label{from-allozymes-to-dna-sequences-and-the-adh-locus}

While allozymes provided a first glimpse of molecular variation, they
detected only a subset of amino-acid changes and gave no information
about synonymous or noncoding variation. DNA sequencing changed this.
Kreitman's 1983 study of nucleotide polymorphism at the \emph{Drosophila
melanogaster} alcohol dehydrogenase (\emph{Adh}) locus was among the
first direct views of DNA-level polymorphism in a natural population,
revealing extensive synonymous and nonsynonymous
variation\textsuperscript{190}. \emph{Drosophila} was well-positioned
for these early molecular studies in part because its giant polytene
chromosomes --- visible in larval salivary glands --- had long allowed
cytogeneticists to map genes and inversions directly onto physical
chromosome structure\textsuperscript{206}. This cytogenetic foundation
identified conserved chromosome arms across \emph{Drosophila} species
(Muller's elements), providing a comparative scaffold that would later
anchor genome-wide sequence comparisons --- one of the earliest examples
of what we now call comparative genomics\textsuperscript{206}.

The \emph{Adh} locus illustrates the vocabulary of molecular variation
clearly. At some sites, individuals within \emph{D. melanogaster} differ
from each other --- these are \textbf{polymorphisms} (segregating
sites). At other sites, \emph{D. melanogaster} carries one allele while
related species (\emph{D. simulans}, \emph{D. yakuba}) carry another,
but variation is absent within each species --- these are \textbf{fixed
differences}\textsuperscript{189}. Comparing the ratio of nonsynonymous
to synonymous variants at polymorphic sites versus fixed differences
between species forms the basis of the McDonald--Kreitman test, one of
the most widely used tests for detecting adaptive protein
evolution\textsuperscript{190}.

More broadly, nucleotide sequence data from many loci established that:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Most nonsynonymous variants are rare within populations, consistent
  with purifying selection removing them.
\item
  A small fraction of loci show elevated diversity at intermediate
  frequencies, consistent with balancing selection maintaining multiple
  alleles.
\item
  A substantial component of molecular evolution in some taxa (e.g.,
  \emph{Drosophila}) appears driven by positive selection, while in
  others (e.g., humans) adaptive substitutions appear less frequent.
\end{itemize}

These single-locus insights set the stage for asking the same questions
across entire genomes\textsuperscript{190,205}.

\subsection{The omics era and the rise of population
genomics}\label{the-omics-era-and-the-rise-of-population-genomics}

High-throughput sequencing technologies transformed population genetics
into population genomics. This transition into the ``omics era'' is
characterized by large-scale, quantitative, and integrative
analyses\textsuperscript{188}. Genome sequencing of non-model organisms
is now routine, and whole-genome resequencing of many individuals per
species enables true population genomics: simultaneous analysis of
polymorphism and divergence across every part of the
genome\textsuperscript{188}.

This genomic perspective enables researchers to ask questions that were
impossible with single loci:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  What fraction of the genome evolves under purifying selection versus
  neutrally?
\item
  How prevalent are adaptive substitutions genome-wide?
\item
  What demographic events --- bottlenecks, expansions, admixture ---
  have shaped a population's history, and where are their genomic
  signatures?
\item
  How does recombination rate variation shape the landscape of diversity
  and differentiation?
\end{itemize}

One striking insight from these surveys is that neutral diversity
\(\pi\) varies over a far narrower range across species than census
population sizes would predict\textsuperscript{205}. In a survey of 167
species across 14 phyla by Leffler et al.~(2012), \(\pi\) ranged only
about 800-fold --- from the Eurasian lynx (\(\pi \approx 0.01\%\), or
roughly 1 difference per 10,000 bases) to the sea squirt \emph{Ciona
savignyi} (\textasciitilde1 difference per 12 bases) --- even though
census population sizes span many more orders of
magnitude.\textsuperscript{189,205} This ``old riddle'' suggests that
forces beyond census size --- including natural selection reducing
effective population sizes --- constrain genetic diversity, and it
remains an active research frontier\textsuperscript{205}.

\section{Evolutionary Processes and Genomic Patterns of
Variation}\label{evolutionary-processes-and-genomic-patterns-of-variation}

Classical population genetics provides simple null models for how allele
and genotype frequencies behave under specified assumptions, and
population genomics extends these ideas across whole genomes. The goal
in this section is to connect key statistics --- \(\pi\), Tajima's D,
and \(F_{ST}\) --- to the underlying evolutionary processes and to show
how these forces leave recognizable signatures in genomic
data\textsuperscript{188,189}. It is worth noting that many of these
calculations can be on genomics datasets using toolkits like
\textbf{VCFtools} introduced in Chapter 3, working directly with VCF
files.

\subsection{Hardy--Weinberg equilibrium: a null model for genotype
frequencies}\label{hardyweinberg-equilibrium-a-null-model-for-genotype-frequencies}

The simplest population model assumes random mating, infinite population
size, and no mutation, migration, or selection. Under these conditions,
genotype frequencies are entirely predictable from allele frequencies
--- a result known as \textbf{Hardy--Weinberg equilibrium
(HWE)}\textsuperscript{189}.

Consider a biallelic locus where allele \(A_1\) is at frequency \(p\)
and allele \(A_2\) is at frequency \(q = 1 - p\). In a randomly mating
population, gametes fuse independently, so the probability of drawing
two \(A_1\) copies is \(p \times
p = p^2\). The three genotype frequencies are therefore:

\[
P(A_1A_1) = p^2, \quad P(A_1A_2) = 2pq, \quad P(A_2A_2) = q^2.
\]

A key subtlety is that we only need to assume \textbf{random mating at
the focal locus} for these frequencies to hold among newly formed
zygotes\textsuperscript{189}. Natural selection, genetic drift, and
other evolutionary processes can be acting elsewhere in the genome
without disrupting Hardy--Weinberg at any given locus, as long as
individuals mate without regard to their genotype at that location. This
is why HWE often holds remarkably well in natural populations:
individuals do not mate globally at random, but they typically do mate
at random with respect to the genotype at most individual
loci\textsuperscript{189}.

\textbf{Departures from HWE are informative:} An excess of homozygotes
relative to HWE expectations (i.e., a deficit of heterozygotes) can
arise from inbreeding, positive assortative mating, or population
subdivision (the Wahlund effect). An excess of heterozygotes can arise
from disassortative mating or balancing selection\textsuperscript{189}.
In bioinformatics pipelines, HWE tests are also used as quality control:
large-scale deviations at many loci can indicate genotyping errors,
sample contamination, or data artifacts rather than real biology.

\textbf{Generalized HWE and inbreeding:} When related individuals mate,
their offspring can inherit two copies of the same allele descended from
a common ancestor. We call such alleles \textbf{identical by descent
(IBD)}, and an individual carrying them is said to be \textbf{homozygous
by descent} or \textbf{autozygous}\textsuperscript{189}. We quantify
inbreeding using the \textbf{inbreeding coefficient} \(F\), the
probability that both alleles in an individual are IBD. When \(F > 0\),
genotype frequencies deviate from standard HWE in a predictable way:

\[
P(A_1A_1) = (1-F)p^2 + Fp, \quad
P(A_1A_2) = (1-F)\,2pq, \quad
P(A_2A_2) = (1-F)q^2 + Fq.
\]

Inbreeding inflates homozygote frequencies and reduces heterozygosity.
In conservation genetics this matters enormously: the Mexican wolf
(\emph{Canis lupus baileyi}), reduced to just five wild individuals
before a captive breeding program was established, now has an estimated
average inbreeding coefficient of \(\hat{F} \approx 0.33\), meaning
roughly a third of each wolf's genome is homozygous by
descent\textsuperscript{189}.

\textbf{Runs of homozygosity:} Because related parents transmit alleles
in large intact blocks --- recombination has had few generations to
break up IBD segments --- inbred individuals show long genomic
\textbf{runs of homozygosity (ROH)}: stretches of the genome where an
individual is homozygous at essentially every SNP\textsuperscript{189}.
The proportion of the genome in ROH segments (\(F_{ROH}\)) estimates the
inbreeding coefficient, and the length distribution of ROH encodes
timing information: very long ROH reflect recent inbreeding, while many
shorter ROH reflect accumulation over many
generations.\textsuperscript{189} In a study of 2,500 dogs across many
breeds, Doberman Pinschers showed more genome in very long ROH
(reflecting recent intensive breeding), while English bulldogs had more
shorter ROH (reflecting a longer cumulative
history)\textsuperscript{189}. ROH analysis is now standard in
conservation and livestock genomics.

\subsection{Measures of genetic variability at the sequence
level}\label{measures-of-genetic-variability-at-the-sequence-level}

When we sequence DNA from multiple individuals, several complementary
statistics summarize the genetic variation we observe. I have recorded a
\href{https://auburn.hosted.panopto.com/Panopto/Pages/Viewer.aspx?id=bf9c8b7c-92e2-436d-8ddf-b40a0139e33b}{video
explanation} of how to calculate several of the measures introduced
below.

\textbf{Nucleotide diversity (\(\pi\)):} The most widely used measure is
\textbf{nucleotide diversity \(\pi\)}, defined as the average number of
pairwise nucleotide differences per site between two randomly chosen
sequences from the population\textsuperscript{189}. If at site \(i\) the
derived allele has estimated frequency \(\hat{p}_i\) across \(L\) sites,
a convenient estimator is:

\[
\hat{\pi} = \frac{1}{L} \sum_{i=1}^{L} 2\hat{p}_i(1 - \hat{p}_i).
\]

Under a standard neutral model with constant effective population size
\(N_e\) and per-site mutation rate \(\mu\) per generation, the expected
value is:

\[
E[\pi] = 4N_e\mu.
\]

This relationship is fundamental: it means \(\pi\) provides a window
into the product \(\theta = 4N_e\mu\), sometimes called the
\textbf{population-scaled mutation rate}. Species with larger long-term
\(N_e\) are expected to harbor more diversity, because more individuals
means more opportunities for new mutations to arise and persist before
being lost to drift\textsuperscript{189}.

\textbf{Watterson's estimator:} A complementary measure of variation is
the total number of \textbf{segregating sites} \(S\) in the sample. The
number of segregating sites grows with sample size, so we standardize
using \textbf{Watterson's estimator}:

\[
\hat{\theta}_W = \frac{S}{a_n}, \quad \text{where } a_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}
\frac{1}{k}.
\]

Both \(\hat{\pi}\) and \(\hat{\theta}_W\) estimate the same underlying
quantity \(\theta = 4N_e\mu\) under the standard neutral model, but they
weight variants differently. \(\hat{\pi}\) gives more weight to variants
at intermediate frequency (because those contribute more to pairwise
differences), while \(\hat{\theta}_W\) gives equal weight to every
segregating site, including rare singletons. This difference is the
foundation of Tajima's D\textsuperscript{190}.

\textbf{The site frequency spectrum:} Beyond counting polymorphic sites,
we can ask about the \textbf{distribution of allele frequencies} across
sites --- a summary called the \textbf{site frequency spectrum
(SFS)}\textsuperscript{189}. We count how many sites in our sample have
a derived allele frequency of \(1/n\), \(2/n\), \(3/n\), and so on up to
\((n-1)/n\). Alleles found in only one copy are called
\textbf{singletons}; those in two copies, \textbf{doubletons}, and so
on. Under neutrality with constant population size, the SFS has a
characteristic shape: many rare variants and fewer variants at high
frequency. Deviations from this shape encode information about
demographic history and selection, and the SFS underlies many of the
most powerful modern methods for demographic inference.

\subsection{Genetic drift and effective population
size}\label{genetic-drift-and-effective-population-size}

\textbf{Genetic drift} is the random change in allele frequencies caused
by the finite number of individuals that contribute genes to the next
generation\textsuperscript{189,205}. In any generation, only a sample of
all possible gametes actually form the next generation, and by chance
some alleles leave more descendants than others --- regardless of their
fitness effects. The strength of drift is inversely proportional to
population size: in a large population, random fluctuations average out
and allele frequencies change slowly; in a small population, random
changes can be large.

The clearest consequence of drift is the \textbf{loss of heterozygosity}
over time. In the absence of new mutations, drift will eventually fix
one allele and eliminate all others. The rate of this loss is:

\[
H_t = \left(1 - \frac{1}{2N_e}\right)^t H_0 \approx H_0\, e^{-t/2N_e},
\]

where \(H_0\) is the initial heterozygosity and \(H_t\) is
heterozygosity after \(t\) generations\textsuperscript{189}. For a
population of \(N_e = 1{,}000\), heterozygosity falls to about 37\% of
its original value after roughly 2,000 generations. For \(N_e = 100\),
the same decline takes only \textasciitilde200 generations.

The conservation implications are stark. The black-footed ferret
(\emph{Mustela nigripes}) crashed to just 18 individuals in 1985 (of
which only 7 reproduced), causing a sharp drop in heterozygosity that is
still visible today even after the population has recovered to over 300
individuals.\textsuperscript{189} Because all living black-footed
ferrets are descended from those 7 founders, genetic diversity remains
low and this reduced variation limits the population's long-term
adaptive potential.

\textbf{Effective population size (\(N_e\)):} Real populations rarely
behave like an idealized constant-size population of \(N\) individuals
all contributing equally to reproduction. Variance in reproductive
success, fluctuations in census size, unequal sex ratios, and geographic
structure all cause genetic drift to proceed faster than the census size
\(N\) would suggest. The \textbf{effective population size} \(N_e\) is
defined as the size of an idealized Wright--Fisher population that would
experience the same rate of random allele-frequency change as the real
population\textsuperscript{189}. Almost always, \(N_e < N\).

\(N_e\) is strongly affected by population bottlenecks. Because the
harmonic mean of a set of numbers is dominated by the smallest values, a
population that numbers one million individuals 99\% of the time but
crashes to 1,000 every hundred generations will have an \(N_e\) far
closer to 1,000 than to one million.\textsuperscript{189} For humans,
the global census size exceeds 8 billion, but \(N_e\) estimated from
genomic diversity is only about 10,000--30,000, reflecting ancient
bottlenecks (including the out-of-Africa dispersal) and variance in
reproductive success\textsuperscript{189,205}.

Importantly, \(N_e\) also differs among parts of the genome. Autosomes,
the X chromosome, the Y chromosome, and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) have
different modes of inheritance and different sensitivities to variance
in male versus female reproductive success\textsuperscript{189}. In many
animal species, fewer males than females reproduce successfully (e.g.,
in harem-forming species), which reduces the effective number of
contributing Y chromosomes relative to mtDNA. A striking demonstration
comes from ancient horse DNA: comparing Scythian (2,300 year-old) to
modern horses, levels of Y chromosome diversity collapsed far more
dramatically than mtDNA diversity, reflecting intense selection of a
small number of stallions during domestication\textsuperscript{189}.

\textbf{Mutation--drift balance:} When drift removes variation while
mutation continually introduces new alleles, these forces can reach a
dynamic equilibrium. At equilibrium, the expected heterozygosity is:

\[
H \approx 4N_e\mu = \theta,
\]

the same population-scaled mutation rate estimated by \(\hat{\pi}\) and
\(\hat{\theta}_W\). Notice that diversity depends on the \emph{product}
of \(N_e\) and \(\mu\), not on either alone. This is partly why species
with similar census sizes can have very different \(\pi\), and why the
narrow range of \(\pi\) across species with very different census sizes
is so puzzling --- additional factors such as linked selection (see
below) must be suppressing \(N_e\) in large-census-size species.

\subsection{Tajima's D and departures from the standard neutral
model}\label{tajimas-d-and-departures-from-the-standard-neutral-model}

\textbf{Tajima's D} exploits the fact that \(\hat{\pi}\) and
\(\hat{\theta}_W\) estimate the same \(\theta\) under the standard
neutral model but are sensitive to different parts of the allele
frequency distribution\textsuperscript{189}. A
\href{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wiyay4YMq2A}{great video
explanation} of Tajima's D and its relation to the site frequency
spectrum was recorded a while back by my own PhD Mentor Dr.~Mohamed
Noor. The statistic is calculated according to the following formula:

\[
D = \frac{\hat{\pi} - \hat{\theta}_W}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\pi} -
\hat{\theta}_W)}}.
\]

When the site frequency spectrum matches neutral expectations,
\(D \approx 0\). Departures in either direction are informative:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Negative \(D\)} (excess of rare variants): occurs after recent
  population expansion (new mutations enter as singletons), after a
  recent positive selective sweep (nearby variation is eliminated and
  then regenerates as rare variants), or under ongoing purifying
  selection\textsuperscript{188,189}.
\item
  \textbf{Positive \(D\)} (deficit of rare variants, excess at
  intermediate frequencies): occurs after a population bottleneck (rare
  alleles are lost preferentially), or under balancing selection (which
  actively maintains alleles at intermediate frequencies for long
  periods)\textsuperscript{188,189}.
\end{itemize}

Empirical examples anchor these interpretations. Genome-wide Tajima's D
in many human populations tends to be slightly negative, consistent with
recent population expansion that produced many new rare
variants\textsuperscript{205}. Maize (\emph{Zea mays}), domesticated
from wild teosinte roughly 10,000 years ago, shows a shift toward
positive Tajima's D relative to teosinte, consistent with the
domestication bottleneck eliminating rare alleles and enriching
intermediate-frequency variants\textsuperscript{189}. At loci under
balancing selection --- such as some MHC immune-gene loci in vertebrates
--- local Tajima's D can be strongly positive with elevated \(\pi\)
compared to neighboring neutral regions\textsuperscript{189,190}.

In genomic analyses, Tajima's D is typically computed in \textbf{sliding
windows} across chromosomes, producing a landscape of departures from
neutrality that can be compared to recombination rates, gene density,
and functional annotations. Windows with strongly negative \(D\) and
reduced \(\pi\) are candidate selective sweep regions; windows with
strongly positive \(D\) are candidate balancing selection or bottleneck
regions.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Population structure and
\(F_{ST}\)}{Population structure and F\_\{ST\}}}\label{population-structure-and-f_st}

Population subdivision is a pervasive feature of natural populations.
Individuals tend to mate with nearby neighbors rather than with randomly
chosen members of the entire species, and physical or ecological
barriers can further divide populations. The degree to which allele
frequencies have diverged among subpopulations is measured by
\(F_{ST}\)\textsuperscript{190}.

One standard formulation compares heterozygosity within versus across
populations:

\[
F_{ST} = \frac{H_T - H_S}{H_T},
\]

where \(H_T\) is the expected heterozygosity in the total pooled
population and \(H_S\) is the average expected heterozygosity within
subpopulations\textsuperscript{190}. Values range from 0 (no
differentiation; all populations have identical allele frequencies) to 1
(complete fixation of different alleles in different populations, so all
diversity is among populations rather than within them).

\textbf{Intuition from identity by descent:} \(F_{ST}\) can also be
understood through inbreeding. When a population is subdivided, an
individual within one subpopulation is more likely to mate with another
member of the same subpopulation than with a random individual from the
whole species. From the perspective of the total population, individuals
within subpopulations are therefore somewhat ``inbred'' relative to the
global average. \(F_{ST}\) measures the deficit of heterozygosity within
subpopulations compared to the global expectation --- in other words,
the fraction of total genetic variance explained by differences among
populations\textsuperscript{189}.

Under a simple model where one ancestral population of size \(N_e\)
split \(T\) generations ago into two isolated daughter populations with
no subsequent gene flow, \(F_{ST}\) grows over time as drift
differentiates allele frequencies:

\[
F_{ST} \approx \frac{T}{T + 4N_e}.
\]

This shows that differentiation depends on the ratio of divergence time
to \(N_e\): populations diverged long ago, or with small \(N_e\),
accumulate higher \(F_{ST}\).

\textbf{Wright's F-statistics hierarchy:} Wright extended this to a
three-level hierarchy. \(F_{IS}\) measures inbreeding of individuals
relative to their subpopulation; \(F_{ST}\) measures differentiation of
subpopulations relative to the total; \(F_{IT}\) measures overall
inbreeding of individuals relative to the total population. These
satisfy:

\[
(1 - F_{IT}) = (1 - F_{IS})(1 - F_{ST}).
\]

\textbf{Empirical values:} Among major human continental groups,
genome-wide \(F_{ST}\) is typically 0.05--0.15, indicating that most
genetic variation is within, not between,
populations\textsuperscript{205}. Among strongly isolated island
populations or distinct ecotypes, \(F_{ST}\) can exceed
0.3\textsuperscript{188}. Within a species, \(F_{ST}\) can vary sharply
along the genome: regions containing inversions, structural variants, or
loci under divergent selection often show elevated \(F_{ST}\) compared
to the genomic background, making windowed \(F_{ST}\) scans a standard
first step in searching for regions involved in local
adaptation\textsuperscript{188}.

\subsection{Recombination, linkage disequilibrium, and linked
selection}\label{recombination-linkage-disequilibrium-and-linked-selection}

Recombination each generation breaks down associations between alleles
at different loci. The degree of non-random association between alleles
at different loci is called \textbf{linkage disequilibrium (LD)}. For a
pair of biallelic loci with alleles \(A\)/\(a\) and \(B\)/\(b\), the LD
coefficient is:

\[
D_{AB} = p_{AB} - p_A p_B,
\]

where \(p_{AB}\) is the haplotype frequency of
\(AB\)\textsuperscript{189}. If the loci are statistically independent,
\(D = 0\). LD decays over time as:

\[
D_t = (1 - c)^t D_0,
\]

where \(c\) is the recombination fraction between the two
loci\textsuperscript{189}. For tightly linked loci, LD can persist for
thousands of generations; for loci on different chromosomes
(\(c = 0.5\)), LD is halved every generation. A striking demonstration
of LD decay comes from Neanderthal admixture: modern Eurasians carry
\textasciitilde1--4\% Neanderthal-derived sequence, and LD between
Neanderthal-ancestry alleles in modern Europeans decays exponentially
with genetic distance in a way consistent with admixture
\textasciitilde35,000--47,000 years ago\textsuperscript{189}.

In practice, LD is often summarized using \(r^2\), the squared
correlation of allele states between loci. Genome sequences and linkage
maps together reveal highly heterogeneous recombination landscapes with
hotspots and cold spots\textsuperscript{188}.

\textbf{Linked selection:} Recombination also modulates how selection at
one site affects neutral variation at nearby sites --- a phenomenon
called \textbf{linked selection}. Two major forms
are\textsuperscript{188,189}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Background selection}: Purifying selection against deleterious
  alleles reduces diversity at linked neutral sites. When a deleterious
  allele is eliminated, it drags nearby neutral variation to extinction
  along with it.
\item
  \textbf{Selective sweeps}: Positive selection on a beneficial allele
  causes nearby neutral variation to ``hitchhike'' to high frequency or
  fixation, reducing diversity in a window around the selected site.
\end{itemize}

In regions of low recombination, both forms can substantially depress
neutral diversity, creating ``cold spots'' in the landscape of \(\pi\)
even when mutation rates are not unusually
low\textsuperscript{188,189,205}. In \emph{Drosophila}, neutral
diversity is often lowest near centromeres and telomeres, consistent
with strong background selection and sweeps in low-recombination
regions\textsuperscript{188}. This has a practical consequence for
interpreting population genomic scans: a dip in \(\pi\) near a gene does
not necessarily mean \emph{that} gene was the direct target of selection
--- it may simply be in LD with a nearby selected site.

\subsection{Natural selection: how fitness differences change allele
frequencies}\label{natural-selection-how-fitness-differences-change-allele-frequencies}

\textbf{Natural selection} changes allele frequencies non-randomly,
based on fitness differences among genotypes. We quantify these
differences using the \textbf{selection coefficient} \(s\), which
measures the difference in relative fitness between
alleles\textsuperscript{189}.

In the simplest case --- a haploid population where allele \(A_1\) has
fitness 1 and \(A_2\) has fitness \(1 - s\) --- the frequency of \(A_1\)
after \(\tau\) generations starting from initial frequency \(p_0\) is
approximately:

\[
p_\tau \approx \frac{p_0}{p_0 + q_0\, e^{-s\tau}}.
\]

This logistic equation produces the classic S-shaped trajectory of a
beneficial allele rising toward fixation. The allele increases slowly
when rare (it is mostly in heterozygotes, where its advantage may be
diluted), accelerates as it becomes common, then slows again as the
alternate allele nears loss.

\textbf{How long does a sweep take?} The time for a beneficial allele to
rise from a single copy to near-fixation in a population of size \(N\)
is approximately:

\[
\tau \approx \frac{2}{s}\log(N).
\]

For a selection coefficient of \(s = 0.01\) (a 1\% fitness advantage) in
a population of \(N = 10{,}000\), this is about 1,840 generations. The
real-world example of \textbf{lactase persistence} in humans illustrates
this well: the allele allowing lactase expression in adults was absent
in Central Europe more than 5,000 years ago and is now at frequencies
above 70\% in many European populations, consistent with a strong
selection coefficient (\(s \approx 0.01\)--\(0.05\)) that arose with
dairy farming\textsuperscript{189}.

\textbf{Diploid selection and dominance.} In diploid organisms, the
fitness of a heterozygote need not be intermediate between the two
homozygotes. The \textbf{dominance coefficient} \(h\) captures this:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Genotype & \(A_1A_1\) & \(A_1A_2\) & \(A_2A_2\) \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Fitness & \(1\) & \(1 - hs\) & \(1 - s\) \\
\end{longtable}

When \(h = 0\), allele \(A_1\) is fully dominant (the heterozygote has
the same fitness as the better homozygote). When \(h = 1\), \(A_1\) is
fully recessive\textsuperscript{189}. Dominance profoundly affects how
selection acts on rare alleles: a recessive beneficial allele is nearly
invisible to selection when rare because it is almost always found in
heterozygotes.

\textbf{Balanced polymorphisms:} Not all selection drives alleles to
fixation or loss. When heterozygotes have higher fitness than either
homozygote --- \textbf{heterozygote advantage} or overdominance ---
selection maintains both alleles at a stable equilibrium. The classic
example is sickle-cell anemia: heterozygotes are protected from malaria
relative to both the normal homozygote (malaria susceptible) and the
sickle-cell homozygote (severe anemia). A second compelling example
comes from Soay sheep: two alleles at the \emph{RXFP2} locus affect horn
size, with each homozygote suffering fitness costs at different
life-history stages (viability vs.~reproductive success), while
heterozygotes achieve the highest combined fitness\textsuperscript{189}.
Both alleles are maintained at intermediate frequency, and this type of
locus shows elevated \(\pi\) and positive Tajima's D --- the genomic
signature we expect under balancing selection.

\subsection{Drift, migration, and demographic
history}\label{drift-migration-and-demographic-history}

Genetic drift and migration jointly shape the distribution of variation
within and among populations. Drift reduces diversity over time and can
fix neutral or mildly deleterious alleles; migration (gene flow) tends
to homogenize allele frequencies and counteract
differentiation\textsuperscript{189}. Their interplay generates a
spectrum of patterns from smooth \textbf{isolation-by-distance} clines
--- where genetic differentiation increases gradually with geographic
separation --- to sharp \textbf{contact zones} between diverging
lineages\textsuperscript{188}.

Population genomics leverages whole-genome data to reconstruct
\textbf{demographic histories} by examining the site frequency spectrum,
distributions of pairwise coalescence times, and patterns of haplotype
sharing\textsuperscript{188}. Bottlenecks, expansions, and admixture all
leave characteristic genomic signatures. Because these signatures can
sometimes resemble those produced by selection at particular loci, it is
essential to account for demography when interpreting outlier regions in
genome-wide scans.

\textbf{Coalescent theory} provides the formal framework for relating
patterns of genomic variation to demographic history by reasoning
backward in time\textsuperscript{189}. Rather than tracking allele
frequencies forward through generations, coalescent theory asks: looking
backward, when did the ancestors of our sampled sequences last share a
common ancestor? This event is called a \textbf{coalescence}. In a
population of effective size \(N_e\), the expected coalescence time for
a pair of lineages is \(2N_e\) generations. For a sample of \(k\)
lineages, the expected time until the first coalescence event is:

\[
E[T_k] = \frac{2N_e}{\binom{k}{2}}.
\]

The total expected time to the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of all
\(n\) sampled sequences is approximately \(4N_e(1 - 1/n)\) generations.
A key insight is that neutral mutations do not affect the coalescent
process --- they are simply scattered onto the coalescent tree at
random. This means we can think about the tree structure first (shaped
by drift and demography) and then superimpose mutations (shaped by
mutation rate)\textsuperscript{189}.

Long-term changes in population size alter coalescence rates in
predictable ways. A recent population bottleneck accelerates coalescence
(many lineages find common ancestors rapidly in the recent past), while
population expansion slows it (lineages are slow to coalesce in the
larger ancestral population). Methods such as PSMC, SMC++, and
fastsimcoal2 exploit these relationships to infer detailed demographic
histories from genomic data.

Under the island-mainland model --- a small island population of size
\(N_I\) receiving migrants from a large mainland at rate \(m\) per
generation --- differentiation between island and mainland reaches an
equilibrium where:

\[
F_{IM} = \frac{1}{1 + 4N_I m}.
\]

This elegant result shows that even a small number of migrants per
generation (\(N_I m \gtrsim 1\)) is enough to substantially suppress
differentiation. The key parameter is not the migration rate alone, but
the product of effective population size and migration rate.

In Lab 10, you will use an R Shiny app that I built based on 1000
Genomes data to visualize sliding‑window estimates of \(F_{ST}\),
\(\pi\), and Tajima's D across several human genomic regions that were
generated using VCFtools. For each assigned region, you will:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Examine windowed \(F_{ST}\) between population pairs to identify peaks
  of differentiation.\\
\item

\item

\end{itemize}

This lab provides a concrete example of how the summary statistics

\section{Sliding Window Analyses, Genome-wide Scans, and Data
Challenges}\label{sliding-window-analyses-genome-wide-scans-and-data-challenges}

Population genomics often proceeds by scanning the genome for regions
where summary statistics deviate from a background pattern, then asking
what biological processes might explain those deviations. Sliding‑window
approaches are central to this strategy: they smooth noisy site‑level
statistics, highlight clusters of extreme values, and provide a natural
bridge between population‑genetic theory and genome
annotation\textsuperscript{188,207}.

In a sliding‑window analysis, the genome is divided into consecutive
windows, defined either by physical distance (for example, 50 kb) or by
a fixed number of SNPs (for example, 100 variants). A statistic of
interest---such as mean \(F_{ST}\), average \(\pi\), or Tajima's D---is
calculated in each window, and the window is then moved along the
chromosome, often with overlap, to produce a continuous
profile\textsuperscript{207}. Because evolutionary processes such as
selection and linked selection typically affect stretches of the genome
rather than isolated sites, window‑based statistics are well suited to
detecting their footprints.

Different evolutionary scenarios lead to characteristic window‑level
signatures. Regions affected by recent positive selection in one
population may show a local reduction in \(\pi\), negative Tajima's D,
and elevated \(F_{ST}\) compared to the genome‑wide background. Regions
under balancing selection can show elevated \(\pi\) and positive
Tajima's D, and sometimes lower \(F_{ST}\) if similar polymorphisms are
maintained across populations. Regions strongly influenced by background
selection may display reduced \(\pi\) without dramatic changes in
\(F_{ST}\) or Tajima's D\textsuperscript{188,207}. Genome‑wide scans
exploit these patterns by computing many such statistics in windows and
then flagging windows that fall in the tails of their empirical
distributions.

Haasl and Payseur review a wide variety of statistics used in
genome‑wide scans for selection and emphasize that no single metric is
definitive\textsuperscript{207}. Site‑frequency‑based tests (such as
Tajima's D), haplotype‑based tests, and differentiation measures (like
\(F_{ST}\) or related quantities) each respond differently to selection
and demography. Combining them can increase power and specificity. For
example, a region with high \(F_{ST}\) but otherwise unremarkable
\(\pi\) and Tajima's D might reflect drift or demographic history,
whereas a region with high \(F_{ST}\), strongly reduced \(\pi\) in one
population, and negative Tajima's D is more consistent with a localized
selective sweep.

Practical choices about window design matter. Larger windows average
over more sites, reducing sampling noise but potentially diluting narrow
signals of selection; smaller windows increase resolution but yield
noisier estimates and more extreme values by
chance\textsuperscript{207}. Windows defined by physical distance align
naturally with gene models and recombination maps, while SNP‑based
windows equalize the number of variants per window but can span very
different physical lengths in regions of high or low SNP density.
Overlapping windows produce smoother profiles but create strong
correlations among neighboring windows; non‑overlapping windows reduce
this correlation but may slice through true
signals\textsuperscript{207}.

Once candidate windows have been identified, the next step is to connect
them to biological features. A typical workflow is to merge adjacent
outlier windows into broader candidate regions, intersect these regions
with gene annotations and regulatory elements, and then prioritize genes
based on known functions, expression patterns, or previous association
and QTL studies\textsuperscript{188,207}. In many systems, such
genome‑wide scans have successfully highlighted loci involved in traits
such as high‑altitude adaptation, host--pathogen interactions,
pigmentation, and domestication.

\subsection{Missing data, ascertainment, and robustness of window-based
scans}\label{missing-data-ascertainment-and-robustness-of-window-based-scans}

The reliability of sliding‑window analyses depends strongly on data
quality and study design. Missing genotypes, uneven coverage, and
ascertainment bias can all distort estimates of \(F_{ST}\), \(\pi\),
Tajima's D, and related statistics\textsuperscript{207,208}. These
issues are particularly important in reduced‑representation datasets
(such as RADseq, GBS, and SNP chips), low‑coverage sequencing, and
ancient DNA.

Missing data arise for many reasons. Random dropout, low read depth, and
sequencing errors can cause some genotypes to be uncalled or miscalled.
Reduced‑representation methods sample only a subset of the genome by
design, often with allele dropout at polymorphic restriction sites. Some
variants may also be effectively ``missing'' because they occur in
unsampled or extinct ``ghost'' populations that have contributed
ancestry to the sampled groups\textsuperscript{208}. Each of these
mechanisms can affect window‑based statistics in different ways.

Systematic differences in coverage or missingness among populations can
bias between‑population statistics. If one population has lower average
depth or a higher fraction of missing genotypes, variant callers may
preferentially retain high‑frequency alleles in that population, making
it appear less diverse and exaggerating \(F_{ST}\) in some
windows\textsuperscript{207,208}. Ascertainment bias---such as SNPs
discovered in a subset of populations and then genotyped elsewhere---can
skew the site frequency spectrum, reducing the apparent number of rare
variants and altering \(\hat{\theta}_W\), \(\hat{\pi}\), and Tajima's
D\textsuperscript{207}.

Common responses to missing data include discarding sites or individuals
with too much missingness, treating missing genotypes as random and
ignoring them in likelihood calculations, or imputing missing genotypes
from reference panels or local haplotype structure\textsuperscript{208}.
These strategies can work reasonably well when missingness is modest and
approximately random, but can introduce biases when missingness is
structured across populations or along the genome. Recent work has
developed corrected estimators of summary statistics that explicitly
account for genotyping errors and missing data, and methods that
integrate missingness into demographic or selection
models\textsuperscript{208}.

For sliding‑window analyses, these considerations suggest several best
practices. Filters on depth, genotype quality, and call rate should be
applied consistently across populations, and sensitivity analyses should
be used to check whether apparent peaks in \(F_{ST}\) or dips in \(\pi\)
are robust to reasonable changes in filtering
thresholds.\textsuperscript{207} Where possible, neutral simulations or
resampling approaches that reproduce the observed missing‑data pattern
can be used to assess how often similar extrema would arise by
chance\textsuperscript{207,208}. Interpreting outlier windows is most
convincing when statistical signals align with regions of good data
quality and with independent evidence from gene function, expression, or
other genomic features.

Overall, sliding‑window analyses, genome‑wide scans for selection, and
careful attention to missing data together form a powerful framework for
reading the evolutionary history of populations from their genomes. The
same summary statistics introduced earlier in the chapter---\(\pi\),
Tajima's D, \(F_{ST}\), and related measures---play central roles in
these analyses, but their interpretation always depends on the
biological context, the demographic background, and the limitations of
the data.

\section{Problems}\label{problems}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Nucleotide diversity and heterozygosity:} Consider a sample of
  \(n\) haploid genomes from a population. For each of \(L\) SNPs, you
  estimate the derived allele frequency \(\hat{p}_i\).

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Write down the estimator of nucleotide diversity \(\hat{\pi}\) in
    terms of the \(\hat{p}_i\). Explain in words what \(\hat{\pi}\)
    measures and how it relates to the concept of expected
    heterozygosity at a locus.\\
  \item
    Suppose that across a set of allozyme loci in a diploid species, the
    average heterozygosity \(\bar{H}\) is 0.12. What does this imply
    about the expected fraction of loci at which a randomly chosen
    individual is heterozygous?\\
  \item
    In a resequenced 1 kb gene region, you estimate
    \(\hat{\pi} = 0.004\) per site. How would you compare this gene's
    diversity to the genome‑wide allozyme heterozygosity estimate, and
    what additional context would you need to make a fair comparison?
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{Interpreting Tajima's D:} You compute Tajima's D in 10 kb
  windows across a genome and observe many windows with strongly
  negative D values.

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Describe at least two evolutionary scenarios (one demographic, one
    selective) that could produce genome‑wide negative Tajima's D.\\
  \item
    How might you distinguish between these scenarios using additional
    statistics or data (e.g., recombination maps, functional
    annotations, or outgroup comparisons)?\\
  \item
    In a specific genomic region, you observe negative Tajima's D
    together with markedly reduced \(\pi\) relative to the genomic
    background. Under what conditions would you interpret this as
    evidence for a recent selective sweep?
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{\(F_{ST}\) and genomic landscapes of differentiation:} You
  have whole‑genome SNP data from two partially isolated populations.
  You compute windowed \(F_{ST}\) (100 kb windows) and find that most
  windows have low \(F_{ST}\) (\textasciitilde0.05), but a small
  fraction have much higher values (\textgreater0.3).

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Describe at least two possible explanations for these
    high‑\(F_{ST}\) windows (one involving selection, one involving
    neutral processes).\\
  \item
    How could you use additional statistics such as \(\pi\), \(d_{XY}\),
    and Tajima's D to help distinguish between these explanations?\\
  \item
    What role might recombination rate variation play in generating
    heterogeneous \(F_{ST}\) across the genome?
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{Sliding windows vs.~spline‑based windows:} You are designing a
  genome‑wide scan for selection using pooled sequencing data from two
  populations and SNP‑wise \(F_{ST}\) estimates.

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Compare fixed‑size sliding windows (e.g., 50 SNPs per window) with
    the spline‑based windowing implemented in GenWin. What are the main
    advantages and disadvantages of each approach?\\
  \item
    In a simulation study, you find that spline‑based windows with the
    \(W\) statistic yield a higher true‑positive to false‑positive ratio
    than fixed windows, even though both approaches detect a similar
    number of true selected regions. Explain why this might be the
    case.\\
  \item
    Describe how you would use neutral simulations or permutation tests
    to determine an empirical significance threshold for \(W\) in your
    dataset.
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{Missing data and summary statistics:} Consider a
  reduced‑representation dataset (e.g., RADseq) with substantial missing
  data and variable coverage across individuals and populations. You
  wish to estimate windowed \(\pi\) and \(F_{ST}\).

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Discuss at least two ways in which missing data can bias estimates
    of \(\pi\) and \(F_{ST}\), particularly when missingness differs
    systematically among populations.\\
  \item
    How might you modify your analysis to mitigate these biases (e.g.,
    filtering strategies, using genotype likelihoods, or correcting
    estimators)?\\
  \item
    Reflect on how the missing data issues discussed here relate to
    earlier chapters on variant calling and GATK's reference confidence
    mode. How do choices made at the variant‑calling stage propagate
    into population genomic analyses?
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  \textbf{Ghost populations and demographic inference:} You are
  analyzing a species with a complex history, including suspected gene
  flow from an unsampled (``ghost'') population.

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Conceptually, explain how unmodeled gene flow from a ghost
    population can bias estimates of \(\pi\), \(F_{ST}\), and Tajima's D
    in the sampled populations.\\
  \item
    Propose one or more strategies (conceptual or methodological) for
    detecting the influence of ghost populations using genomic data.\\
  \item
    How might sliding‑window or spline‑based analyses help you localize
    regions of the genome most affected by ghost admixture?
  \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

\section{Reflection Questions}\label{reflection-questions-10}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{From loci to genomes:} Earlier genetic studies focused on a
  handful of loci, whereas population genomics embraces whole genomes.
  Reflect on how this shift changes the kinds of questions we can ask
  about evolution and how confident we can be in our answers. What new
  challenges arise when moving from a few markers to millions?
\item
  \textbf{Linked selection and interpretation:} Linked selection
  (background selection and selective sweeps) complicates the
  relationship between diversity, recombination, and selection. How does
  this complexity affect our ability to identify specific targets of
  selection? Under what circumstances might you be cautious about
  interpreting low diversity and high \(F_{ST}\) as evidence of local
  adaptation?
\item
  \textbf{Model choice and null expectations:} Many population genomic
  statistics (Tajima's D, \(F_{ST}\), windowed \(\pi\)) are interpreted
  relative to simple null models (e.g., neutrality with constant
  population size). How should we update our ``null expectations'' in
  light of the rich demographic histories and pervasive linked selection
  revealed by genomic data? What does it mean to choose an appropriate
  null model in this context?
\item
  \textbf{Data quality and inference:} Think back to earlier chapters on
  alignment, variant calling, and quality control. In what ways do
  choices made during these early steps constrain or enable the kinds of
  population genomic analyses we can perform? How might you design a
  sequencing and analysis pipeline differently if your primary goal from
  the outset is population genomics rather than variant discovery in a
  single genome?
\item
  \textbf{Ethics and communication:} Population genomics of human
  populations can touch on sensitive issues of ancestry, identity, and
  history. How can scientists responsibly communicate findings about
  human genetic diversity and population structure to avoid reinforcing
  misconceptions or harmful ideologies? What roles do transparency,
  community engagement, and historical context play in this process?
\item
  \textbf{Where to go deeper:} This chapter has provided a conceptual
  overview of population genomics. If you were to take a dedicated
  course in this field, what topics would you be most interested in
  exploring in more depth (e.g., coalescent theory, inference of
  selection, demographic modeling, ancient DNA, graph‑based models of
  population structure)? How might these topics intersect with your own
  research interests or future work?
\end{enumerate}
