\chapter{Lab01: Find and describe a Genome Analysis
Paper}\label{lab01-find-and-describe-a-genome-analysis-paper}

\section{Lab 1}\label{sec-lab01}

In class we will read and discuss a recent genome analysis paper that
illustrates the three perspectives on genomics (cell, organism, tree of
life) and the balance between hypothesis‑driven and discovery‑driven
research introduced in Chapter 1\textsuperscript{1,2,10}.

After class, you will search PubMed for a scientific study that includes
some form of genome analysis. Avoid ``double‑dipping'' by reusing papers
assigned for other courses or lab meetings. Ideally, choose:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  a genome paper on your study organism, or\\
\item
  a paper that follows a workflow similar to one you plan to use in your
  own research, or
\item
  a recent paper that excited you and presents a genome analysis.
\end{itemize}

Before you start, skim the ``Types of Genome Analysis Research
Projects'' section in Chapter 1 and, if needed, review Appendix
Section~\ref{sec-papers} for a refresher on reading primary
literature\textsuperscript{1,2,10,24}.

By the end of this lab, you should be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Identify the main hypothesis (or questions) of a genomics paper.
\item
  Classify the study using the three perspectives from Chapter 1 (cell,
  organism, tree of life).
\item
  Describe whether the study leans more hypothesis‑driven,
  discovery‑driven, or combines both.
\item
  Summarize key genome features (assembly size, chromosome number, basic
  QC metrics) reported in the paper.
\end{itemize}

\section{Deliverables}\label{deliverables}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Paper and methods diagram}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Upload the PDF of your chosen paper to Canvas.\\
  \item
    Upload a one‑page diagram of the methods used to test the main
    hypothesis. Give your diagram a descriptive title and include:

    \begin{itemize}
    \tightlist
    \item
      data types (e.g., short‑read WGS, long‑read assembly, RNA‑seq),\\
    \item
      main analysis steps (alignment, assembly, variant calling,
      comparative analyses),\\
    \item
      which of the three perspectives your paper emphasizes
    \item
      whether it is hypothesis-drive, discovery-based, or both.
    \end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{2--3 minute video summary}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Record an informal 2--3 minute Panopto video summarizing the paper's
    goals, methods, and main findings, and how it fits into the
    perspectives from Chapter 1.
  \item
    Upload the video to the ``Lab Activity \#1'' Panopto assignments
    folder as described on Canvas.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

Please refer to the syllabus for late policies. Detailed step‑by‑step
instructions for recording and uploading Panopto videos are provided on
Canvas rather than here.

\section{Resources and Refreshers:}\label{resources-and-refreshers}

If you do not have much experience finding and reading primary
literature, complete Appendix Section~\ref{sec-papers} (``How to Read
Scientific Literature'') before or alongside this lab. That appendix
walks through hypothesis identification, concept mapping, and designing
follow‑up experiments using a concrete example.

\chapter{Lab02: Design a Genome
Project}\label{lab02-design-a-genome-project}

\section{Lab 2}\label{sec-lab02}

In Chapter 1, we introduced three broad perspectives on bioinformatics
and genomics (cell, organism, tree of life)\textsuperscript{10}. Later
in the textbook, Pevsner expands these 3 perspectives into five basic
perspectives on genome sequencing.

For this lab, you will use these 5 perspectives, along with your new
understanding of sequencing technologies from Chapter 2, to sketch a
1--2 page narrative for a hypothetical genome
project\textsuperscript{10,25,26}.

The five perspectives on genomics discussed in Pevsner Chapter 15 can be
summarized as:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Catalog genomic information}: basic genome features (size,
  chromosomes, GC content, repeats, gene counts), based on sequencing,
  assembly, and annotation.
\item
  \textbf{Catalog comparative genomic information}: whole‑genome
  comparisons to related species, orthologs, divergence times, lateral
  gene transfer, using whole‑genome alignments and genome browsers.
\item
  \textbf{Biological principles}: how genome structure and variation
  underlie development, metabolism, behavior, and evolutionary processes
  (e.g., genome size evolution, polyploidization, gene birth/death).
\item
  \textbf{Human disease relevance}: how genomes relate to disease in
  humans or plants, including SNPs, linkage and association studies, and
  host--pathogen interactions.
\item
  \textbf{Bioinformatics aspects}: databases, software, and
  visualization tools that make genome analysis possible.
\end{itemize}

These map naturally onto the three perspectives in Chapter 1: cell‑scale
questions, organism‑level questions, and tree‑of‑life/comparative
questions\textsuperscript{10}.

\subsection{The Assignment}\label{the-assignment}

Write a 1--2 page narrative of the genome analysis project you have
designed. To guide you, begin by reflecting on the following questions:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{If you could sequence the genomes of 100 individuals from any
  species, which species would you choose?}
\item
  \emph{What hypotheses would you test, how would you perform data
  analyses, and what resources would you require in terms of hardware,
  software, and collaborators?}
\item
  \emph{What ethical issues might arise in sequencing these genomes?}
\end{itemize}

Specifically, think about:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Which sequencing platforms and coverage would you choose (Chapter 2)?
\item
  Which file formats and QC steps would your workflow rely on (Chapter
  3)?\textsuperscript{10,25,26}
\end{itemize}

For your design narrative:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Choose a species and justify why 100 genomes from this species would
  be informative. - State one or two main hypotheses, or guiding
  questions if discovery-based.
\item
  Identify which of the five perspectives (and which of the three
  Chapter 1 perspectives) your project emphasizes.
\item
  Outline your sequencing strategy (platforms, approximate coverage,
  sample types) using concepts from Chapter 2.
\item
  Sketch the main analysis steps (from raw FASTQ through
  alignment/assembly and downstream analyses) using ideas from Chapters
  1 and 3.
\item
  Briefly note any major ethical issues if humans or other sensitive
  species are involved.
\end{itemize}

The focus of your design narrative should be on \textbf{motivation and
approach}. You may refer to assigned readings
(e.g.,\textsuperscript{1};\textsuperscript{2};\textsuperscript{3}) in
your narrative, but you do not need a formal reference list.

\section{References}\label{references-12}

\chapter{Lab04: Genome Sequence Indexing and
Alignment}\label{lab04-genome-sequence-indexing-and-alignment}

\chapter{Lab05: BLAST on the Command
Line}\label{lab05-blast-on-the-command-line}

For this lab, you will learn to use BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search
Tool) on the command line to identify sequence homology and annotate
unknown sequences. While web-based BLAST is convenient for single
queries, command-line BLAST is essential for analyzing large datasets,
automating repetitive tasks, and integrating BLAST into bioinformatics
pipelines. This lab will walk you through creating BLAST databases,
running searches, and parsing results---skills that are fundamental to
genome annotation, comparative genomics, and evolutionary studies.

\section{Background: Why Command Line
BLAST?}\label{background-why-command-line-blast}

BLAST is the most widely used bioinformatics tool, with the original
publication cited nearly 80,000 times\textsuperscript{63}. While the web
interface at NCBI is user-friendly, command-line
BLAST\textsuperscript{64} offers several advantages:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Batch processing}: Query thousands of sequences automatically
\item
  \textbf{Custom databases}: Search against your own sequences, not just
  NCBI's databases
\item
  \textbf{Reproducibility}: Scripts can be shared and rerun exactly
\item
  \textbf{Integration}: Combine BLAST with other tools in analysis
  pipelines
\item
  \textbf{Control}: Fine-tune parameters and output formats for
  downstream analysis
\end{itemize}

In this lab, you'll work with a \textbf{realistic scenario}: you've
assembled transcripts from a newly sequenced plant genome and need to
annotate them using the well-characterized \emph{Arabidopsis thaliana}
genome. Your goal is to determine which transcripts correspond to
mitochondrial, chloroplast, or nuclear genes.

  \item

  \end{itemize}
\item
  Open \texttt{Example\_script.sh} in your preferred text editor. This

  commands to it as you progress, building a complete, reusable BLAST
  workflow by the end.
\item
  Replace your username at the top:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\VariableTok{DIR}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"/home/aubclsfXXXX/Lab5"} \CommentTok{\# Replace with your username}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\end{enumerate}

\section{Step 1: Examine Your Query
Sequences}\label{step-1-examine-your-query-sequences}

Before running BLAST, you should understand your input data.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Use \texttt{less} to view the \texttt{test.fasta} file. Recall that
  FASTA format consists of a header line starting with
  \texttt{\textgreater{}} followed by the sequence on subsequent lines.
\item
  Count how many sequences are in \texttt{test.fasta}.

  \textbf{Hint}: The \texttt{\textgreater{}} symbol marks each new
  sequence header. Use \texttt{grep} with the \texttt{-c} flag to count
  matching lines. Check \texttt{man\ grep} if needed.
\item
  Record this number---you'll need it later to determine how many
  sequences had no BLAST hits.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Step 2: Create BLAST
Databases}\label{step-2-create-blast-databases}

When you use BLAST on the NCBI website, you're searching against
pre-built databases. To use BLAST on the command line with custom
sequences, you must first build your own databases.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Load the BLAST module to access the BLAST+ tools:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{module}\NormalTok{ load blast+/2.15.0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Examine the database creation tool:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{makeblastdb} \AttributeTok{{-}help}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  Look through the documentation to identify the required parameters.
  Key options include:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \texttt{-in}: Input FASTA file
  \item
    \texttt{-dbtype}: Type of sequences (\texttt{nucl} for nucleotides,
    \texttt{prot} for proteins)
  \item
    \texttt{-out}: Output database name (optional; defaults to input
    filename)
  \end{itemize}

  \begin{quote}
  Documentation on this module can be found on the
  \href{https://hpcdocs.asc.edu/content/blast}{ASC Documentation Site}.
  Additional documentation on this tool can be found
  \href{https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK52640/}{at NCBI}.
  \end{quote}
\item
  Determine the sequence type in your FASTA files. Open one of the
  \texttt{AT*.fasta} files with \texttt{less}. Are these nucleotide or
  protein sequences?
\item
  Create a BLAST database for each of the three \emph{Arabidopsis}
  sequence files (\texttt{ATcp.fasta}, \texttt{ATmt.fasta}, and
  \texttt{ATchrV.fasta}). Do \textbf{not} create a database from
  \texttt{test.fasta}---this will be your query.

  For example, for the chloroplast:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{makeblastdb} \AttributeTok{{-}in}\NormalTok{ ATcp.fasta }\AttributeTok{{-}dbtype}\NormalTok{ nucl}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  \textbf{Tip}: To make your script more flexible, use variables as
  shown in the example script. For instance:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\VariableTok{cp}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ATcp.fasta}
\ExtensionTok{makeblastdb} \AttributeTok{{-}in} \VariableTok{$cp} \AttributeTok{{-}dbtype}\NormalTok{ nucl}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Add these three \texttt{makeblastdb} commands to your
  \texttt{Example\_script.sh} file.
\item
  Submit your script to the ASC queue with these parameters:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Number of CPUs = 1
  \item
    RAM/Memory = 50MB
  \item
    Queue = class
  \item
    Time = 01:00:00 (1 hour)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  After the job completes, check the standard output file (ending in
  \texttt{.o} followed by the job number) for errors. Then list your
  directory contents.
\item
  You should now see multiple new files for each database (with
  extensions like \texttt{.nhr}, \texttt{.nin}, \texttt{.nsq}, etc.).
  These are the indexed database files that BLAST will use for rapid
  searching. Count how many new files were created per input FASTA file.
\item
  Check your job efficiency using \texttt{jobinfo\ -j\ JOBNUMBER}. Note
  the memory and CPU usage---this information helps you optimize future
  jobs. What was your memory efficiency? CPU efficiency?
\end{enumerate}

\section{Step 3: Run Your First BLAST
Search}\label{step-3-run-your-first-blast-search}

Now you'll compare your unknown transcripts \texttt{test.fasta} against
each of the three databases you created. First, examine
Figure~\ref{fig-blast} to determine which program to use within BLAST.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, rightrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, toprule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Programs within BLAST}, left=2mm, colback=white, bottomtitle=1mm, toptitle=1mm, bottomrule=.15mm, coltitle=black, titlerule=0mm, breakable, opacityback=0, arc=.35mm]

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.65\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{images/Figure4_2.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-blast}Overview of BLAST five main Algorithms}

\end{figure}%

There are five major algorithms within BLAST. In making your database,
you already know your input sequences are nucelotides. Example the input
file \texttt{test.fasta} to determine which of the five programs you
will use when running your BLAST search.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Since both your query and database sequences are nucleotides, you'll
  use the \texttt{blastn} program. Review the available options:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{blastn} \AttributeTok{{-}help}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  The essential parameters are:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \texttt{-query}: Your input FASTA file
  \item
    \texttt{-db}: The database to search against
  \item
    \texttt{-out}: Output file name
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Run BLAST to compare \texttt{test.fasta} against the chloroplast
  database. For example:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{blastn} \AttributeTok{{-}query}\NormalTok{ test.fasta }\AttributeTok{{-}db}\NormalTok{ ATcp.fasta }\AttributeTok{{-}out}\NormalTok{ test\_vs\_cp.blastn\_out}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  Use a descriptive output filename that indicates the query and
  database (e.g., \texttt{test\_vs\_cp.blastn\_out} for test query
  versus chloroplast database).
\item
  Repeat for the other two databases (mitochondrial and chromosome V).
  Add all three BLAST commands to your script.
\item
  Submit your updated script to the queue:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Number of CPUs = 1
  \item
    RAM/Memory = 100MB
  \item
    Queue = class
  \item
    Time = 01:00:00
  \end{itemize}

  \begin{quote}
  \textbf{Tip}: After successfully creating the blast databases, comment
  out the \texttt{makeblastdb} commands (add \texttt{\#} at the start of
  each line) so they don't rerun unnecessarily as we continue to add to
  this script.
  \end{quote}
\item
  Once the job completes, examine one of the output files using
  \texttt{less}. This is BLAST's default ``pairwise'' format, similar to
  what you see on the NCBI website. While human-readable, it's difficult
  to parse computationally.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Step 4: Optimize Output Format for
Parsing}\label{step-4-optimize-output-format-for-parsing}

The default BLAST output is verbose and hard to parse with command-line
tools. BLAST offers alternative formats that are more suitable for
automated analysis.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Review the \texttt{-outfmt} option in the \texttt{blastn\ -help}
  output. You'll see numbered format options (0-18). Formats 6 and 7 are
  tabular and particularly useful for parsing.
\item
  Rerun one of your BLAST searches using \texttt{-outfmt\ 6}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{blastn} \AttributeTok{{-}query}\NormalTok{ test.fasta }\AttributeTok{{-}db}\NormalTok{ ATcp.fasta }\AttributeTok{{-}outfmt}\NormalTok{ 6 }\AttributeTok{{-}out}\NormalTok{ test\_vs\_cp.tab}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Examine the output with \texttt{less}. Format 6 produces tab-delimited
  columns:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Column 1: Query sequence ID
  \item
    Column 2: Subject (database) sequence ID
  \item
    Column 3: Percent identity
  \item
    Column 4: Alignment length
  \item
    Column 5: Number of mismatches
  \item
    Columns 6-12: Additional alignment statistics including E-value
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Compare format 6 to format 7 (which includes column headers). Which do
  you prefer? As a class, decide on one format to use consistently.
\item
  Update your script to use your chosen output format for all three
  BLAST searches. Update the queue parameters based on your previous
  job's runtime and memory usage (check with \texttt{jobinfo}):

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Number of CPUs = 1
  \item
    RAM/Memory = ? (what did you actually use last time?)
  \item
    Queue = class
  \item
    Time = ? (how long did it actually take?)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Comment out the previous BLAST commands and add the new versions.
  Submit to the queue.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Step 5: Understanding Database Size Effects on
E-values}\label{step-5-understanding-database-size-effects-on-e-values}

The E-value (expect value) represents the number of hits you'd expect to
see by chance in a database of this size. Larger databases generally
produce larger E-values for the same match.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  To avoid duplicating large files, I have pre-downloaded Chr1 of the
  \emph{Arabidopsis} genome. You'll create a symbolic link to the
  database folder (make sure to replace your username as you did during
  setup):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{ln} \AttributeTok{{-}s}\NormalTok{ /home/aubclsfXXXX/bioinf\_shared/Arabidopsis\_thaliana/CHR\_I}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  A symbolic link acts like a shortcut---the files appear in your
  directory but remain stored in the original location.
\item
  BLAST allows you to search multiple databases simultaneously by
  listing them in quotes:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{blastn} \AttributeTok{{-}db} \StringTok{"ATcp.fasta ATchrV.fasta CHR\_I/NC\_003070.fasta ATmt.fasta"} \DataTypeTok{\textbackslash{}}
  \AttributeTok{{-}query}\NormalTok{ test.fasta }\AttributeTok{{-}outfmt}\NormalTok{ 6 }\AttributeTok{{-}out}\NormalTok{ combined\_search.txt}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  This searches all four databases (chloroplast, chrV, chrI, and
  mitochondrial) in one run.

  \begin{quote}
  Note: If you named your BLAST databases something different than the
  default names, then you will need to edit this to match your database
  naming conventions here.
  \end{quote}
\item
  Add this command to your script, comment out previous lines, and
  submit to the queue with updated parameters.
\item
  After completion, compare the E-values for a specific hit:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Find a transcript that matched the chloroplast in your earlier
    single-database search
  \item
    Look up the same transcript in your combined search output
  \item
    How did the E-value change? Why? \textbf{Consider}: The combined
    database is much larger than the chloroplast alone.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\section{Step 6: Parse BLAST Output to Count Hits Per
Database}\label{step-6-parse-blast-output-to-count-hits-per-database}

Now you'll use command-line text processing tools to extract meaningful
summaries from your BLAST results. The goal is to count how many of your
query transcripts match each database (mitochondrial, chloroplast, or
nuclear chromosomes). You will be making a long one-liner with multiple
piped steps that you will build incrementally below.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Your BLAST output columns 1 and 2 contain the query name and database
  hit. Extract just these columns using \texttt{awk}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ExtensionTok{blastn} \AttributeTok{{-}db} \StringTok{"ATcp.fasta ATchrV.fasta CHR\_I/NC\_003070.fasta ATmt.fasta"} \DataTypeTok{\textbackslash{}}
  \AttributeTok{{-}query}\NormalTok{ test.fasta }\AttributeTok{{-}outfmt}\NormalTok{ 6 }\KeywordTok{|} \FunctionTok{awk} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}\{print $1,$2\}\textquotesingle{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  The \texttt{\textbar{}} (pipe) sends BLAST output directly to
  \texttt{awk} without creating an intermediate file. In the next
  several steps, add each command via pipe to this command line
  argument. In the end, you will redirect the output to a file.

  \begin{quote}
  Keep in mind that if you run the command above by itself, the output
  will be LARGE! So if you want to test each step of your piped
  one-liner, simplify the output by piping it to \texttt{head}
  periodically. But \textbf{beware}! Do not accidentally leave a
  \texttt{\textbar{}\ head\ \textbar{}} in the middle of your one-liner
  which will effectively remove a vast majority of your output hits!
  \end{quote}
\item
  Each query might have multiple hits to the same database sequence.
  Remove duplicates with another pipe to \texttt{sort} and then
  \texttt{uniq} to yield unique query-database pairs (one line per
  transcript-database match).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
Hint: Do not forget to use the man page when needed to remind yourself
how to use these tools.
\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\item
  Now focus only on which databases were hit by adding a pipe to awk to
  isolate only column 2. This will remove the query names.
\item
  Next, count how many times each database appears by piping the output
  to \texttt{uniq\ -c} (which requires sorted input).
\item
  Sort the counts numerically and save to a file called
  \texttt{RawCounts.txt}.
\item
  Examine \texttt{RawCounts.txt}. You should see counts for each
  database. Did you get more hits to chromosome I (the full chromosome)
  or to chromosome V (partial)? Why might that be?
\item
  Both chrV and chrI should be ``NT'', but since we used a symbolic link
  for chrI, it shows up differently in our output. Use \texttt{sed} to
  convert chrI hits to \textbf{\emph{NT}} so we can combine hits for
  these two chromosomes.
\item
  Add this complete one-liner to your script. This is a powerful example
  of piping multiple tools together---a common pattern in
  bioinformatics.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Step 7: Identify Sequences with No BLAST
Hits}\label{step-7-identify-sequences-with-no-blast-hits}

Some of your query transcripts may not match any database, suggesting
they could be novel genes, misassembled sequences, or contamination.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Sequences with no BLAST hits won't appear in your output file at all.
  Calculate the number:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Total sequences in \texttt{test.fasta} (you counted this in Step 1)
  \item
    Minus: Number of sequences with at least one hit
  \end{itemize}
\item
  To count sequences with hits, extract unique query IDs from your BLAST
  output:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{awk} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}\{print $1\}\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{ combined\_search.txt }\KeywordTok{|} \FunctionTok{sort} \KeywordTok{|} \FunctionTok{uniq} \KeywordTok{|} \FunctionTok{wc} \AttributeTok{{-}l}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\item
  Calculate:
  \texttt{(total\ sequences)\ -\ (sequences\ with\ hits)\ =\ sequences\ with\ no\ hits}
\item
  Alternatively, if you want to know which specific sequences had no
  hits, you could:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Extract all sequence IDs from \texttt{test.fasta}:
    \texttt{grep\ "\textgreater{}"\ test.fasta\ \textgreater{}\ all\_queries.txt}
  \item
    Extract hit IDs from BLAST output:
    \texttt{awk\ \textquotesingle{}\{print\ \$1\}\textquotesingle{}\ combined\_search.txt\ \textbar{}\ sort\ \textbar{}\ uniq\ \textgreater{}\ hit\_queries.txt}
  \item
    Find the difference:
    \texttt{comm\ -23\ all\_queries.txt\ hit\_queries.txt}
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Add the count of sequences with no hits to the bottom of your
  \texttt{RawCounts.txt} file using \texttt{echo}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\BuiltInTok{echo} \StringTok{"No hits: [your count]"} \OperatorTok{\textgreater{}\textgreater{}}\NormalTok{ RawCounts.txt}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
\end{enumerate}

\section{Step 8: Finalize Your
Script}\label{step-8-finalize-your-script}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Review your \texttt{Example\_script.sh}. It should now contain:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Commands to create three BLAST databases
  \item
    Commands to run BLAST searches (with appropriate output formatting)
  \item
    A one-liner to parse results and count hits per database
  \item
    Calculation of sequences with no hits
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Add comments throughout your script to explain what each section does.
\item
  Test that your script runs successfully from start to finish. You can
  do this by:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Removing all output files
  \item
    Resubmitting the script (with all commands uncommented)
  \item
    Verifying all expected outputs are generated
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

This script is now a reusable tool. With minor modifications, you could
use it to annotate sequences from any organism against any reference
genome.

\section{References}\label{references-13}

\chapter{Lab06: HMMs in Predicting Gene
Models}\label{lab06-hmms-in-predicting-gene-models}

Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are a set of mathematical tools that can be
used to draw inferences about genomic and evolutionary processes. In
general, an HMM calculates the probability of each scenario that could
have resulted in an observed data set, then uses statistical methods to
determine which scenarios are most likely to have occurred. For example,
HMMs can be applied to DNA sequence data from different species to infer
the likely pattern of relationships among those species.

\section{Learning Goals}\label{learning-goals-1}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Students will understand the basic structure of an HMM, the types of
  data used in ab initio gene prediction, and its consequent
  limitations.
\item
  Students will understand the process of gene exon-intron boundary
  prediction, having altered the values for the key parameters and noted
  the impact on the prediction.
\item
  Students will consider how the exon-intron boundary model might be
  designed to be more accurate, thinking about the biological features
  of the process and how they might be represented in a computer
  program.
\end{itemize}

\section{Learning Objectives}\label{learning-objectives-2}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Students will be able to process unannotated genomic data using ab
  initio gene finders as well as other inputs.
\item
  Students will be able to defend the proposed gene annotation.
\item
  Students will reflect on the other uses for HMMs.
\end{itemize}

\section{Step-by-Step Instructions:}\label{step-by-step-instructions}

\subsection{Part 1: Reviewing the

The first part of this lab activity reviews some of the concepts
introduced in \hyperref[hidden-markov-models-in-biology]{Chapter 9} on
how HMMs work to predict a specific gene model based on a DNA sequence.

\subsection{Part 2: Exploring an HMM}\label{part-2-exploring-an-hmm}

For the next part of the lab, we will use an excel spreadsheet provided
by Anton Weisstein to explore properties of Hidden Markov Models. The
Excel workbook ``Hidden Markov Model'' illustrates the mathematical
workings of an HMM, using the example of locating the 5' splice site
within a DNA sequence (see
\hyperref[hidden-markov-models-in-biology]{Chapter 9} for more detail).
By manipulating model parameters such as the average length and base
composition of introns vs.~exons, the user can study how such changes
influence the model's decisions about where the splice site is likeliest
to occur. For ease of demonstration, the workbook begins by analyzing a
very short sequence (6 bp) before re-creating Eddy's full, 26-bp
model\textsuperscript{4}.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Download and open the excel file
  ``\href{datasets/Hidden\%20Markov\%20Model.intron.xls}{HiddenMarkovModel.intron.xls}''.
  Before changing any of the sliders on the spreadsheet, save a copy of
  the file under a different name.
\item
  The first sheet in the workbook, appropriately named ``Simple Model'',
  demonstrates the calculations involved in building an HMM to determine
  the exact location of an exon/intron boundary. The user enters a short
  DNA sequence and sets model parameters. The workbook then uses these
  values to compute the likelihood of each potential 5' splice site
  location.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Cells \textbf{B2--B4} contain the probabilities that the DNA
    sequence begins in different regions of a gene. In HMM parlance,
    these regions are described as states of the model.
  \item
    Cells \textbf{F4--I6} give the probability per nucleotide of moving
    from one state to another. For example, if G4 = 0.60, then a
    nucleotide in the gene's exon has a 60\% chance of being followed by
    a nucleotide in the splice site. This model focuses only on 5'
    splice sites, so states will always occur in the order Exon --
    Splice -- Intron -- End.
  \item
    Cells \textbf{F12--I14} give the state-specific probability of
    producing, or emitting, a particular nucleotide. In the initial
    model, all four nucleotides are equally likely to occur in an exon,
    but introns are GC-poor. For the sake of simplicity, the splice site
    is considered to be only one nucleotide long: in the initial model,
    that nucleotide is always a guanine.\\
  \item
    Finally, Cells \textbf{B17--G17} contain the nucleotide sequence to
    be analyzed.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Cells \textbf{B21--L51} show the model's calculations. For each
  potential state path, the model computes:

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\roman{enumii}.}
  \item
    the probability that the DNA sequence starts in the appropriate
    state,
  \item
    the probability of precisely following the state path, and
  \item
    the probability of emitting the observed DNA sequence if the state
    path is followed.
  \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

For example, state path 1 (Cells \textbf{B21--H21}) posits that the
first nucleotide, a cytosine, occurs in an intron. The initial model
gives a 0\% probability of starting in an intron (Cell \textbf{B4}), and
a 10\% frequency of cytosines within an intron (Cell \textbf{G14}), so
these values are reported. The second nucleotide, a guanine, is also
proposed to occur in an intron. The initial model therefore reports the
90\% probability of remaining within an intron (Cell \textbf{H6}) and
the 10\% frequency of guanines within an intron (Cell \textbf{H14}).
This process continues through all six nucleotides, then reports the
10\% probability of transitioning from the last nucleotide's state ---
an intron --- to the end of the sequence (Cell \textbf{I6}).

\begin{itemize}
\item
  HMMs assume that each nucleotide is \textbf{independent} of the
  others, much as the result of a coin flip does not depend on previous
  or future flips. This assumption of independence is biologically
  unrealistic, but it greatly simplifies the math: each nucleotide's
  individual probabilities can be simply \textbf{multiplied} together to
  calculate the total probability of the overall sequence. For state
  path 1, this combined probability is reported in Cell \textbf{J22}.
  Unsurprisingly, given that one of the numbers being multiplied was
  zero, the resulting product is also zero, meaning that this state path
  is not consistent with the observed sequence. In fact, under the
  initial model, state paths 3 and 5 are the only ones possible, because
  only they correctly place the splice site at a G.
\item
  Computationally, it is faster to add numbers together than to multiply
  them. This can make a huge difference when running a large HMM that
  may contain many millions of state paths. For this reason, most HMMs
  calculate the combined probability of a state path not by multiplying
  the individual nucleotide probabilities, but by \textbf{adding the
  logarithms} of those probabilities, using the identity. The resulting
  log-probabilities are reported in Column K. Note that ln(0) is
  undefined, so state paths with probability zero yield an error message
  in this column.
\item
  If the model correctly includes all possible state paths, adding up
  all of the probabilities in \textbf{Column J} should give the total
  probability p of emitting the observed sequence. But by definition,
  that sequence has indeed been observed, so the individual state path
  probabilities should be calibrated to \textbf{sum to one}. (In much
  the same way, if I have prior knowledge that a poker player is holding
  either a flush or a full house, each of those two hands is much
  likelier than if I lacked such knowledge.) Each state path's
  probability is therefore divided by the total probability p to compute
  the path's likelihood given observed DNA sequence. The results are
  displayed in \textbf{Column L} (which does sum to 1) and graphed in
  the \textbf{likelihood profile} at the bottom of the worksheet.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\emph{Now that we have reviewed how this worksheet works, let's
perturb it to better understand WHY it works!}}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}

  Record in the table below how these perturbations affect the

\subsection{Part 3: Model
Perturbations}\label{part-3-model-perturbations}

In this part of the lab, you will explore how modifications to the HMM
affect its predictions. Choose \textbf{at least one} of the following
explorations (items 1-4), document the changes you make, and record the
resulting effects on the model's splice site predictions. For each
exploration you choose, you should test multiple parameter values to
observe trends, not just a single change.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Change the observed DNA sequence.} Alterations in GC richness
  and in the position of any G nucleotides may influence the likelihood
  of the 5' splice site occurring at a specific position. Note that the
  sequence must consist only of standard DNA nucleotides (A, C, G, and
  T).

  \emph{Suggestion: Try sequences with different numbers of G's and/or
  different GC content (e.g., GC-rich vs.~AT-rich).}
\item
  \textbf{Change the base emission probabilities for exon and/or intron
  states.} Alterations in the base composition of exons vs.~introns will
  affect the model's inferences about the best splice site position. In
  particular, changing the emission probabilities so that exons and
  introns have similar base compositions will severely degrade the
  model's ability to predict the splice site location with any degree of
  confidence.

  \begin{quote}
  Note that each position within a given gene region must be occupied by
  one of the four nucleotides, so each row of the emission probability
  matrix must sum to one. If this condition is violated, the offending
  row will be highlighted in red.
  \end{quote}

  \emph{Suggestion: Try making introns more GC-rich or making exons and
  introns compositionally similar.}
\item
  \textbf{Change the state transition probabilities using the built-in
  scrollbars.} Again, each row of the transition matrix must sum to one.

  \begin{quote}
  Note that the transition probability (p) for the exon state to the
  splice site state is the reciprocal of the average exon length. (This
  is because the mean of a geometric distribution is 1/p.) For example,
  if the transition probability for the exon-to-splice site state is
  10\%, then the average exon will be 10 bp long. Similarly, the
  intron-to-end transition probability is the reciprocal of the average
  intron length. Adjusting these parameters will therefore shift the
  most likely splice site position to earlier or later in the sequence.
  The model assumes that the splice site consists of a single
  nucleotide, so the probabilities in the middle row cannot be changed.
  \end{quote}

  \emph{Suggestion: Experiment with different average exon and intron
  lengths by adjusting transition probabilities. What happens with very
  short vs.~very long predicted gene features?}
\item
  \textbf{Change the vector of initial state probabilities.} The
  original model assumes that the DNA sequence starts in an exon (100\%
  probability in cell B2). However, the start of the DNA sequence could
  be part of an intron or even at the splice site itself. A better model
  should account for this possibility and assign non-zero initial
  probabilities to all three states.

  \begin{quote}
  Note that, by definition, the sequence must start in one of these
  three states and these initial probabilities must sum to one.
  \end{quote}

  \emph{Suggestion: Try splitting the initial probability equally among
  all three states, or giving higher probability to intron starts.}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{For the exploration you choose to conduct document:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The specific parameter(s) you changed and the values you tested
\item
  The effect on the predicted splice site position(s)
\item
  The effect on the likelihood values
\item
  Your interpretation of why these changes had the observed effects
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Part 4: Exploration of the Full
Model}\label{part-4-exploration-of-the-full-model}

The second sheet of the ``Hidden Markov Model'' workbook contains an
exact replica of the HMM described by Eddy (2004)\textsuperscript{4}.
This sheet can be reached using the navigation tabs at the bottom of the
Excel workspace. Eddy's HMM is designed to handle DNA sequences up to 26
bp in length; moreover, under the initial settings, the splice site can
occur at either an A or a G, although the latter is far more likely.

\textbf{Key differences from the Simple Model:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Handles sequences up to 26 nucleotides instead of just 6
\item
  The splice site can occur at either an A or a G (though G is far more
  likely)
\item
  You can paste sequences directly into Cell E16 rather than entering
  individual nucleotides
\item
  The likelihood profile shows more nuanced predictions across a longer
  sequence
\item
  Additional calculations are available in separate worksheets for those
  interested in the mathematical details
\end{itemize}

This sheet's controls work similarly to the Simple Model. The interface
is streamlined to focus on the model's controls and output graph. If you
want to examine the detailed calculations, scroll down to Rows 44--183
or navigate to the ``Additional Calculations'' sheet.

\textbf{Exploratory Activity:} Choose \textbf{ONE} exploration from the
options below. Test multiple parameter values or sequences to observe
trends and patterns. Document what you changed, what happened, and your
interpretation of the results.

\subsubsection{Option 1: Base Composition
Effects}\label{option-1-base-composition-effects}

Investigate how the compositional difference between exons and introns
affects splice site prediction. Start with the default settings where
exons have equal base frequencies (25\% each) and introns are AT-rich
(A=40\%, T=40\%, G=10\%, C=10\%).

Systematically change the emission probabilities to make introns less
AT-rich (more similar to exons). Test at least 3-4 different scenarios
ranging from strong contrast to no contrast. For each scenario, record
which position is predicted as the splice site and the maximum
likelihood value.

\textbf{Key questions to explore:} How much compositional difference is
needed for confident predictions? What happens when exons and introns
have identical base composition?

\subsubsection{Option 2: Sequence
Variation}\label{option-2-sequence-variation}

Test how different DNA sequences are interpreted by the model while
keeping all parameters constant. Generate or find at least 3-4 different
26 bp sequences with varying characteristics (GC-rich, AT-rich, multiple
G's in different positions, random sequences, or real genomic
sequences).

For each sequence, note its GC content, where G nucleotides are located,
and where the model predicts the splice site.

\textbf{Key questions to explore:} Does the model always pick the first
G? What happens with closely spaced G's? How important is the position
of G nucleotides versus overall sequence composition?

\subsubsection{Option 3: Species-Specific Gene
Architecture}\label{option-3-species-specific-gene-architecture}

Research typical exon and intron lengths for a specific organism
(budding yeast, fruit fly, human, arabidopsis, or another of your
choice). Use online databases like NCBI Gene, Ensembl, or model organism
databases to find this information for several genes.

Calculate average lengths and convert them to transition probabilities
using the formula: self-transition probability ≈ (average length - 1) /
(average length). Enter these organism-specific values into the model
and observe how predictions change.

\textbf{Key questions to explore:} How do your organism's gene
architecture parameters differ from the defaults? What would happen if
you used a yeast-trained HMM to predict human genes, or vice versa?

\subsubsection{Option 4: Statistical Power
Analysis}\label{option-4-statistical-power-analysis}

Explore the relationship between base composition difference and
prediction confidence. Create a series of tests where you systematically
vary the AT content difference between exons and introns (e.g., 30\%,
20\%, 10\%, 5\%, 0\% difference).

For each level of difference, record the maximum likelihood value from
the profile. You might create a simple graph (by hand or in Excel)
showing how prediction confidence changes as compositional difference
decreases.

\textbf{Key questions to explore:} At what compositional difference does
prediction confidence drop below 50\%? Is there a threshold where the
model essentially ``gives up'' and spreads probability across many
positions?

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\tightlist

\item

\item
  What happened in each test (predicted positions and approximate
  likelihoods)
\item
  Patterns or trends you observed
\item

\end{itemize}

\section{Reflection Questions}\label{reflection-questions-13}

Now that you've completed the lab, reflect on the following questions.
Your answers should demonstrate understanding of HMM principles and
their application to gene prediction.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Parameter sensitivity}: Based on your systematic explorations
  in Part 2 (transition probabilities and emission probabilities), which
  type of parameter seems to have the strongest effect on splice site
  prediction accuracy? Explain your reasoning using specific examples
  from your completed tables. How does this relate to the way real gene
  prediction software is trained?
\item
  \textbf{Model complexity trade-offs}: The toy model in this lab uses
  just three states (Exon, Splice, Intron) and models the splice site as
  a single nucleotide with strong G preference. Real gene finders like
  AUGUSTUS use dozens of states and model splice sites with
  position-specific weight matrices spanning multiple nucleotides. What
  are the advantages and disadvantages of increasing model complexity?
  Consider factors like:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Prediction accuracy
  \item
    Amount of training data required
  \item
    Computational cost
  \item
    Risk of overfitting
  \item
    Interpretability
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Integration with other data}: In question 6 of Part 2, you
  considered how RNA-Seq data could help resolve ambiguous splice site
  predictions. Describe in detail how you would integrate RNA-Seq
  evidence with HMM-based predictions. What would you look for in the
  RNA-Seq data? How would you handle cases where they disagree?
\item
  \textbf{Simple versus Full Model}: Compare your experience working
  with the Simple Model (6 bp, Part 2) versus the Full Model (26 bp,
  Part 4). What additional insights did the longer sequence provide?
  What made the Full Model more challenging or interesting to work with?
  How does the increased sequence length affect the clarity of
  predictions?
\item
  \textbf{Beyond gene prediction}: HMMs are used throughout
  bioinformatics for diverse applications including protein domain
  identification (profile HMMs), sequence alignment (pair HMMs), and
  ancestry inference (as discussed in
  \hyperref[hidden-markov-models-in-biology]{Chapter 9}). Choose one
  application of HMMs from the chapter that is NOT gene prediction and
  explain:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    What are the ``states'' in that application?
  \item
    What are the ``observations'' (emissions)?
  \item
    Why is an HMM appropriate for that problem?
  \item
    How is it similar to or different from the gene prediction HMM you
    worked with in this lab?
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\chapter{Lab07: Variant Calling via GATK Best
Practices}\label{lab07-variant-calling-via-gatk-best-practices}

\section{Overview and Learning
Objectives}\label{overview-and-learning-objectives}

The primary goal of most NGS workflows is to generate high-quality
genetic variants for downstream biological analysis. However, as you
learned in \textbf{Chapter 10}, raw NGS data is inherently noisy,
containing sequencing errors, PCR duplicates, and alignment artifacts
that can generate thousands of false-positive variant calls. Without
careful post-processing and filtering, these technical artifacts can
lead to incorrect biological inferences---for example, mistakenly
identifying a sequencing error as a true adaptive mutation in an
experimental evolution study.

This lab walks you through the \textbf{GATK Best Practices workflow}
(see \textbf{Figure 10.1} in Chapter 10) using the \emph{Saccharomyces
cerevisiae} experimental evolution dataset introduced in
\textbf{Appendix C} and first analyzed in \textbf{Lab 4}. You will
complete three major steps:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Post-processing and variant calling}: Mark PCR duplicates,
  call variants using GATK HaplotypeCaller, and assess alignment
  quality.
\item
  \textbf{Hard filtering and quality assessment}: Apply GATK's
  recommended filter thresholds, visualize variant quality
  distributions, and evaluate whether standard cutoffs are appropriate
  for your yeast dataset.
\item
  \textbf{Iterative refinement and comparison}: Adjust filter parameters
  based on quality plots, generate a second filtered callset, and
  compare all three VCFs (raw, GATK-filtered, custom-filtered) using an
  UpSet plot to understand how filtering decisions affect the final
  variant set.
\end{enumerate}

By the end of this lab, you will understand why \textbf{filtering is
iterative and context-dependent}, and you will have hands-on experience
making the kinds of decisions that real genomics researchers face when
balancing sensitivity (retaining true variants) against specificity
(excluding false positives).

\section{Step 2: Variant Filtering}\label{step-2-variant-filtering}

\subsection{Goal}\label{goal-1}

Learn how to filter variants using GATK's \textbf{VariantFiltration}
tool, visualize the distributions of key quality metrics, and evaluate
whether the standard GATK-recommended thresholds are appropriate for
your yeast dataset. This step corresponds to \textbf{Section 10.5 (Hard
Filtering)} and builds your intuition for \textbf{why filtering is
iterative and data-dependent}.

\subsection{Why Filter Variants?}\label{why-filter-variants}

The raw VCF from HaplotypeCaller (\texttt{SRR1693691.SNPs.vcf}) contains
thousands of putative SNPs, but many are false positives caused by
sequencing errors, mapping artifacts, or systematic biases (e.g., strand
bias, where all variant-supporting reads come from one DNA strand).
\textbf{Section 10.5} describes the key quality metrics used for
filtering.

GATK provides \textbf{recommended thresholds} for these metrics (based
on human whole-genome sequencing), but these may not be optimal for
yeast or other organisms. Your task in this step is to apply the
recommended filters, examine the distributions of quality scores, and
decide whether adjustments are needed.

\section{Step 3: Refilter and
Compare}\label{step-3-refilter-and-compare}

\subsection{Goal}\label{goal-2}

Apply your adjusted filter criteria, generate a second filtered callset,
and compare all three VCFs (raw, GATK-filtered, custom-filtered) using
an \textbf{UpSet plot} to visualize the overlaps and differences between
filtering strategies. This step reinforces the key lesson of
\textbf{Section 10.5}: filtering is iterative, context-dependent, and
involves trade-offs.

\subsection{Why Compare Multiple Filtered
Callsets?}\label{why-compare-multiple-filtered-callsets}

In real research, you rarely get filtering right on the first try. By
generating multiple filtered VCFs and comparing them, you can see:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Which variants are robust} (present in all callsets,
  regardless of filter stringency)
\item
  \textbf{Which variants are borderline} (present in permissive filters
  but not strict ones)
\item
  \textbf{How much overlap exists} between GATK's recommended filters
  and your custom filters
\end{itemize}

UpSet plots (introduced in \textbf{Chapter 10} as a superior alternative
to Venn diagrams) show these relationships clearly, especially when
comparing more than two sets.

\subsection{Instructions}\label{instructions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Decide on your adjusted filter criteria}:

  Based on the density plots and tables from Step 2, choose new
  thresholds for \textbf{one or two metrics}. For example:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    If the GATK QD threshold (QD \textgreater{} 2.0) looks too
    permissive (most variants have QD \textgreater{} 10), raise it to QD
    \textgreater{} 5.0.
  \item
    If the FS threshold (FS \textless{} 60.0) excludes very few
    variants, tighten it to FS \textless{} 40.0.
  \end{itemize}

  Write down your new thresholds---you will need them in the next step.
\item
  \textbf{Edit the filtering script to create a second filtered VCF}:

  Open \texttt{6\_GATK\_Variant\_Filtering.sh} again and find the
  \texttt{VariantFiltration} command. \textbf{Copy the entire command}
  and paste it below the original, then modify:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Change the output filename to \texttt{SRR1693691.SNPs.filtered2.vcf}
    (so it doesn't overwrite the first filtered VCF).
  \item
    Adjust the filter expressions (\texttt{-\/-filter-expression} and
    \texttt{-\/-filter-name}) to reflect your new thresholds.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Run the edited script on the ASC. See the suggested queue parameters
  from the first script and make adjustments based on that job run time
  and usage.
\item
  Once you are done, you should now have 3 VCF files:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Raw unfiltered VCF: SRR1693691.SNPs.vcf.gz
\item
  GATK filtered VCF: SRR1693691.SNPs.filtered.vcf
\item
  Your adjusted filtering VCF: SRR1693691.SNPs.filtered2.vcf
\end{itemize}

Now that you have 3 VCF files, you can compare the sets of variants
between the three files using \texttt{vcf-compare}, a tool within
VCFtools. This will generate a text file that can be used to make VENN
diagrams. But of course, we \textbf{\emph{HATE}} VENN diagrams, so

\section{Congratulations!}\label{congratulations}

You have successfully completed the \textbf{GATK Best Practices
workflow} for variant calling and filtering. This lab provides a
real-world experience of the challenges of variant filtering: being too
permissive can lead to false positives (mistaking sequencing errors for
true variants), while being too stringent can exclude real biological
variation. The best practice is to \textbf{experiment with filter
thresholds, examine quality distributions, and err on the side of
caution}---especially for downstream applications where false positives
are costly (e.g., functional validation experiments).

\subsection{Alternative Approaches to
Filtering}\label{alternative-approaches-to-filtering}

As mentioned in \textbf{Section 10.5} and in class, hard filtering is
just one approach to variant quality control. Other methods include:

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Variant Quality Score Recalibration (VQSR)}: A
  machine-learning approach that uses a set of known high-quality
  variants to train a model that distinguishes true variants from
  artifacts. VQSR is the gold standard for human genomics but requires a
  large database of validated variants, making it impractical for
  non-model organisms like yeast. It is also computationally intensive,
  so we do not use it in this course.
\item
  \textbf{Ensemble calling}: Running multiple variant callers (e.g.,
  GATK, FreeBayes, bcftools) on the same data and taking the
  intersection of callsets. Variants called by multiple independent
  algorithms are more likely to be real. You will explore this approach
  in \textbf{Lab 8} when you read benchmarking papers that compare
  different callers.
\item
  \textbf{Empirical validation}: For high-stakes projects (e.g.,
  clinical diagnostics, identifying causal mutations), researchers
  validate a subset of variants using orthogonal methods such as Sanger
  sequencing, high-coverage targeted resequencing, or alternative
  sequencing platforms (e.g., PacBio long reads). If you identify
  100,000 SNPs and want to validate 1\%, that requires validating 1,000
  sites---costly and time-intensive, but sometimes necessary.
\end{itemize}

For most research applications, \textbf{hard filtering combined with
visual inspection in IGV} (which you will do in Lab 9) provides a good
balance between rigor and practicality.

\subsection{Looking Ahead to Lab 9}\label{looking-ahead-to-lab-9}

In the next lab, you will load the filtered VCFs you generated here into
\textbf{IGV (Integrative Genomics Viewer)} along with the aligned BAM
files and the yeast reference genome. You will navigate to specific
SNPs, zoom in to see individual read alignments, and evaluate the
evidence for each variant.

\chapter{Lab08: Beyond GATK -- Benchmarking Variant Calling
Pipelines}\label{lab08-beyond-gatk-benchmarking-variant-calling-pipelines}

\section{Overview}\label{overview-2}

Lab 8 is an \textbf{in-class discussion and synthesis activity} focused
on recent benchmarking studies that compare variant calling pipelines
across different sequencing platforms, organisms, and data types. Over
the past decade, the genomics community has moved beyond asking ``which
tool is best?'' to understanding \emph{when} and \emph{why} different
callers excel, and how upstream choices (alignment, preprocessing,
population ancestry) shape final variant quality. In this lab, you will
critically evaluate five recent papers (2021--2026) that benchmark
variant callers on diverse datasets, extract practical recommendations,
and synthesize guidelines for choosing pipelines in your own
research\textsuperscript{5--9}.

Each student has been assigned one paper based on the first three
letters of their last name (see assignments below). You are expected to
read your assigned paper carefully before class, guided by the questions
provided, and come prepared to contribute to small-group and whole-class
discussions. During class, you will work with peers who read the same
paper to fill out a structured summary table, present key findings to
the class, and collectively build a decision framework for variant
calling that addresses common questions facing genomics researchers.

\section{Pre-Class Preparation: Guiding
Questions}\label{pre-class-preparation-guiding-questions}

As you read your assigned paper, take notes on the following questions.
You will use these notes during the in-class small-group synthesis.

\subsection{Study Design and Scope}\label{study-design-and-scope}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the main goal of the benchmarking study? (e.g., comparing
  germline vs.~somatic callers, evaluating AI-based tools, assessing
  performance on non-model organisms)
\item
  Which datasets were used? (e.g., Genome in a Bottle reference samples,
  monozygotic twins, cancer exomes, specific organisms)
\item
  Which sequencing platforms and read lengths were analyzed? (Illumina
  short reads, PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore, or a mix)
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Tools and Pipelines}\label{tools-and-pipelines}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Which \textbf{aligners} were tested (if applicable)? (e.g., BWA-MEM,
  Bowtie2, minimap2)
\item
  Which \textbf{variant callers} were compared? (e.g., GATK
  HaplotypeCaller, bcftools, FreeBayes, Platypus, DeepVariant, others)
\item
  Did the study evaluate \textbf{ensemble or voting-based methods}? If
  so, how were results combined?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Performance Metrics and
Results}\label{performance-metrics-and-results}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  Which metrics were used to assess performance? (e.g., precision,
  recall, F1-score, concordance with truth sets, computational time,
  memory usage)
\item
  Which tools performed best for \textbf{SNPs}? Which for
  \textbf{indels}?
\item
  Were there differences in performance by \textbf{genomic context}
  (e.g., exonic vs.~intergenic, high-GC regions, repetitive regions)?
\item
  Did computational cost (runtime, memory) play a role in the
  recommendations?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Key Findings and
Recommendations}\label{key-findings-and-recommendations}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{10}
\tightlist
\item
  What are the paper's main recommendations? (e.g., ``use GATK for
  high-coverage human genomes,'' ``ensemble methods reduce false
  positives in somatic calling'')
\item
  Did the authors identify biases or limitations? (e.g., training on
  European-ancestry genomes, poor performance in non-model systems,
  platform-specific errors)
\item
  Are the recommendations generalizable to other organisms, coverages,
  or research questions? Why or why not?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, rightrule=.15mm, leftrule=.75mm, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toprule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Tips for Success}, left=2mm, colback=white, bottomtitle=1mm, toptitle=1mm, bottomrule=.15mm, coltitle=black, titlerule=0mm, breakable, opacityback=0, arc=.35mm]

\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Read your paper thoroughly} before class. Annotate it and

\item
  \textbf{Be ready to explain, not just summarize.} Your classmates will
  rely on you to interpret your paper's findings.
\item
  \textbf{Ask questions during presentations.} Benchmarking studies
  often use different metrics or datasets---clarify what makes results
  comparable.
\item
  \textbf{Think critically about generalizability.} A tool that works
  well for human exomes may fail for non-model organisms or low-coverage
  data.
\end{itemize}

\section{References}\label{references-15}

\chapter{Lab09: IGV Genome Visualization Lab
Activity}\label{lab09-igv-genome-visualization-lab-activity}

\section{Overview}\label{overview-3}

Throughout this course, you have been building a complete NGS
variant-calling workflow using a real experimental evolution dataset. In
Lab 4, you downloaded whole-genome sequencing reads from the
\emph{Saccharomyces cerevisiae} population
SRR1693691\textsuperscript{24}, trimmed them, and aligned them to the
sacCer3 reference genome using BWA to produce a sorted BAM file. In Lab
7, you ran the GATK best practices pipeline on those alignments: you
marked PCR duplicates, called variants with HaplotypeCaller, examined
quality-score distributions using VCFtools density plots, and applied
hard filters to separate high-confidence SNPs from technical noise.
Together, those two labs took you from raw FASTQ files all the way to a
filtered VCF.

This lab is the final step of that journey. Here you will load the same
files---the pre-filtering BAM, the duplicate-marked BAM, and the
unfiltered VCF---into the \textbf{Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV)} and
look at the raw read evidence underneath each variant call. As discussed
in \emph{Chapter 10}, automated filtering is powerful but imperfect:
visual inspection of alignments at candidate variant sites remains an
essential validation step, letting you recognize patterns such as strand
bias, duplicate stacking, and low mapping quality that are difficult to
catch with thresholds alone\textsuperscript{159}. You will also connect
the sequence changes you observe to the biological dataset described in
\textbf{Appendix C}---a pooled yeast population that experienced
hundreds of generations of selection---and reason about whether specific
SNPs could represent adaptive allele-frequency shifts.

By the end of this lab you will be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Load and configure a multi-track IGV session combining a reference
  genome, BAM alignment files, and a VCF.
\item
  Distinguish high-confidence SNPs from likely artifacts based on visual
  read evidence (strand balance, mapping quality, duplicate patterns,
  base quality).
\item
  Apply Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) standardized variant
  nomenclature to describe DNA and protein sequence changes.
\item
  Interpret whether a called SNP falls in a coding region and assess its
  potential amino acid and functional consequences.
\item
  Reflect on how your filtering choices in Lab 7 relate to what you see
  in the read pileups.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\section{Step 1 --- Download and Install
IGV}\label{step-1-download-and-install-igv}

The software IGV is available from the Broad Institute (which also hosts
GATK). IGV stands for \textbf{Integrative Genomics Viewer} and allows
you to upload a variety of genome file formats to view on your desktop
machine. It runs on Java, so you may need to update your version of Java
to run it.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Download IGV from
  \href{https://software.broadinstitute.org/software/igv/downloadLinks}{here}
  (make sure to scroll to the appropriate distribution based on your
  OS). Linux users will download the binary distribution, which can be
  launched directly from the terminal using Java.
\item
  Follow the instructions to install the software on your main OS.
\item
  Make sure after you install it that it loads properly before getting
  started on the exercise below.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Step 2 --- Load Data into IGV}\label{step-2-load-data-into-igv}

The goal of this step is to load the datasets we have worked with in
Labs 4 and 7 into IGV so we can visualize the variants and the read
evidence that supports them. Recall from
\textbf{\href{appendixC.qmd}{Appendix C}} that these files represent a
single \emph{S. cerevisiae} population sequenced from a pooled,
evolve-and-resequence experiment; because the sample is pooled rather
than a single diploid individual, you will see a range of allele
frequencies at variant sites rather than clean 50/100\% het/hom
patterns.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Download files from
  \href{https://auburn.instructure.com/files/275453972/download?download_frd=1}{IGV\_files.zip}
  from Canvas.
\item
  Open IGV. Refer to the slides from this
  \href{https://auburn.hosted.panopto.com/Panopto/Pages/Viewer.aspx?id=51da88a9-e569-4453-b414-b29d0125a0ac}{tutorial}
  if needed throughout.
\item
  First, we need to load the genome file. At the top left, select the
  dropdown menu with the human genome and select the option ``Click for
  more''.
\item
  From the pop-up menu, scroll to the genome for \emph{S. cerevisiae
  (sacCer3)} and click OK to load it into the current session. This is
  the same sacCer3 reference (NCBI assembly R64) you indexed with BWA in
  Lab 4 and used for all downstream analyses.
\item
  Next, at the top left, select ``File'' and ``Load from File'' to
  import your raw sequence alignment (pre-filtering). The file should be
  named \texttt{SRR1693691.sorted.bam} and have a corresponding index
  file named \texttt{SRR1693691.sorted.bam.bai}. Make sure not to select
  the index, but only verify it exists in the same directory. IGV will
  search for it and give an error if it is not there.
\item
  Repeat step 5 on the duplicate-marked BAM file (post-filtering). The
  file should be named \texttt{SRR1693691.markdup.bam} and have a
  corresponding index file named \texttt{SRR1693691.markdup.bai}. As
  discussed in
  \hyperref[variant-calling-and-filtering-with-gatk]{Chapter 10},
  \emph{marking} duplicates rather than removing them lets you see the
  flagged reads in IGV and verify that the duplicate-calling algorithm
  behaved reasonably.
\item
  Finally, you will load the VCF file you generated (pre-filtering). At
  the top left, select ``File'' and ``Load from File'' to import the
  file \texttt{SRR1693691.SNPs.vcf.gz}. This file does not have an index
  but should still load.
\item
  Configure your view in the following ways:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item
    In the sorted BAM panel, right-click and scroll to ``Color
    alignments by'' and in the pull-out menu, select ``read strand''.
    This color-codes reads by forward and reverse, which is essential
    for detecting strand bias---a key artifact signal discussed in
    \hyperref[variant-calling-and-filtering-with-gatk]{Chapter 10}.
  \item
    In the markdup BAM panel, right-click and scroll to ``Duplicates''
    and select ``texture duplicates''. This makes PCR and optical
    duplicates visually distinct rather than hiding them, so you can see
    how many reads at each site are flagged.
  \item
    In the Sequence panel, click to show the standard translation panel
    of the amino acids. This will allow you to determine immediately
    whether a coding SNP changes the amino acid sequence.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  When you are done configuring your session, save it so you can return
  to this configuration in the future. Under ``File'' select ``Save
  Session'' and name your session Lab 9.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Step 3 --- Examine Variants in
Depth}\label{step-3-examine-variants-in-depth}

The goal of this step is to navigate to specific variants and evaluate
the raw read evidence that supports---or does not support---each as a
real, biologically relevant SNP. This mirrors the visual validation
workflow described in
\hyperref[variant-calling-and-filtering-with-gatk]{Chapter 10}, where
IGV is used to recognize artifact patterns (duplicate stacking,
strand-biased reads, low mapping quality, base-end clustering) versus
signatures of a high-confidence true variant (balanced strands, high MQ,
consistent base quality throughout reads).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Now that you have the genome and two BAM tracks loaded into IGV, use
  the tutorial slides as a guide and navigate to the following regions.
  Zoom in enough to see individual reads and any SNP variants validated
  in your VCF:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Region 1: chrII:598117--598156
  \item
    Region 2: chrV:430725--431072
  \item
    Region 3: chrXV:468250--468449
  \end{itemize}
\item
  For each region, answer: how many apparent mismatches (potential
  variants) are visible in the \textbf{raw sorted BAM}? How many remain
  in the \textbf{markdup BAM}? And how many of those are called in the
  \textbf{VCF}? Think about why these three numbers differ.
\item
  For each variant present in the VCF within each window, assess the
  read evidence:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    What is the depth of coverage at that site?
  \item
    Are reads supporting the alternate allele present on both forward
    and reverse strands?
  \item
    Are the supporting bases near the middle of reads (high confidence)
    or clustered at read ends (potential artifact)?
  \end{itemize}

  To better evaluate, sort the reads by base at each variant position:
\item
  Are there any apparent mismatches (or potential sequencing errors) in
  the BAM that are \textbf{not} ``called'' as variants in the VCF? Which
  features of those sites---coverage, strand distribution, read
  position, base quality---might explain why HaplotypeCaller did not
  ``call'' them as variants?
\item
  For the variants that \textbf{are} called in the VCF, based on the
  visual evidence (strand balance, mapping quality, duplicate patterns),
  do you expect that each variant ``Passed'' the hard filters you
  applied at the end of Lab 7? Recall the key thresholds from
  \hyperref[variant-calling-and-filtering-with-gatk]{Chapter 10}: QD
  \textgreater{} 2.0, MQ ≥ 40, FS \textless{} 60, SOR \textless{} 3.0,
  and ReadPosRankSum \textgreater{} −8.0.
\item
  Pick one variant and test your prediction by using \texttt{less} on
  the command line to search for that chromosome and position in your
  filtered VCF file.
\item
  Does the filtered VCF support or reject your prediction? Based on this
  comparison, would you adjust any of your filtering thresholds? In what
  direction, and why?
\item
  For each called SNP in the VCF, return to IGV: is the SNP located
  within a protein-coding exon? Use the gene annotation track and amino
  acid translation track to check.
\item
  If a SNP falls in a coding region, does the nucleotide change alter
  the amino acid? What effect---if any---do you think this amino acid
  change might have on the function of the gene? Remember that variants
  rising to high frequency in this experimental evolution dataset may
  reflect adaptive changes selected over hundreds of generations.
\item
  Using the HGVS naming conventions introduced in
  \hyperref[sequence-alignment]{Chapter 5}, write out the sequence
  changes for each variant you identified:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    A prefix of \textbf{\texttt{g.}} is used for a genomic sequence
    change (e.g., g.69A\textgreater T for an A-to-T substitution at
    genomic position 69).
  \item
    A prefix of \textbf{\texttt{p.}} is used for a protein sequence
    change using the one-letter amino acid code (e.g., p.K23Y for a
    lysine-to-tyrosine substitution at position 23 in the protein).
  \item
    If the SNP is synonymous (silent), note that as well---synonymous
    changes are still described with \texttt{g.} notation.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Feel free to explore additional regions on your own:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    chrII:486633--487123
  \item
    chrV:553052--553399
  \item
    chrXIV:39075--39311
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\section{Deliverables}\label{deliverables-3}

Upload the following to Canvas for a final grade:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Screenshots} of each of the three required regions showing
  your configured view (strand coloring, duplicate texturing, and
  translation track visible).
\item
  \textbf{Written answers} to the questions in Step 3 (questions 2--9),
  clearly numbered.
\item
  \textbf{HGVS variant notation} for each variant you identified in the
  three required regions (question 10), indicating both genomic
  (\texttt{g.}) and, where applicable, protein (\texttt{p.}) level
  changes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

IGV is a powerful way to visually validate specific variants and develop
intuition for what real biological signal looks like versus noise. As
you complete this lab, you are closing the loop on the entire
variant-calling workflow you have built across this course: from raw
FASTQ reads in Lab 4, through alignment and GATK processing in Lab 7, to
biological interpretation here. The ability to move fluidly between a
filtered VCF, the raw read alignments behind it, and the gene annotation
context is a core skill in modern genomics.

\chapter{Lab10: Population Genomics using the 1000 Genomes
Dataset}\label{lab10-population-genomics-using-the-1000-genomes-dataset}

\section{Lab 10: Population Genomics using the 1000 Genomes
Dataset}\label{lab-10-population-genomics-using-the-1000-genomes-dataset}

Today you will be working with human population genomics data from the
\href{https://www.internationalgenome.org/}{1000 genomes project}. The
goal of this exercise is to provide real world experience using
bioinformatics to examine genetic differences within and between
populations.

First, you will be assigned one of five regions (\textasciitilde2-10 Mb
each) that have been targeted due to known signatures of importance in
human evolution. Then, in Part 1, you will explore between population
divergence specific to your region. The examination of these plots and
statistics will be important in selecting populations to examine further
for within population diversity and selection as part of Part 2.
Finally, in Part 3, you will explore your region on the UCSC genome
browser to examine potential genes that may contribute to the population
genetic signal you see in your plots.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

This exercise should provide a sense of how sliding window approaches
are used to identify regions of interest in population genetics studies.
Typically, these scans are done genome-wide along with other statistics
to identify regions of interest. Then, gene annotations are used to find
overlapping functional regions that can explain the genetic patterns.
This can be done programmatically by downloading annotations from UCSC
and using \texttt{bedtools} to intersect with the regions of interest.
Then,
\href{https://genome.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/help/customTrack.html}{custom
tracks} can be used to upload FST, pi, and Tajima's D results to the
genome browser. We will discuss sliding window analyses in more depth in
two weeks.
